modules.title: Product management foundations
modules.summary: Learn how product managers connect strategy, evidence, and outcomes.

blocks.value: What a product manager does

A product manager (PM) helps a team answer three questions. Whose problem should we solve? What should get better for those people? How will we tell whether it did? The PM gathers customer evidence and business needs so the team can make decisions together. Designers lead decisions about how people use the product. Engineers lead decisions about how it works. Operations and launch teams explain what they can deliver and support.

Imagine a grocery app getting more complaints about late orders. The team could immediately build a new tracking screen. First, the PM asks where the delay starts. The answer might point to store preparation, where a tracking screen would have little effect on the actual delay.

value: Compare the recorded times for order acceptance, picking, packing, and courier pickup. A long gap before pickup could indicate that orders are still being packed when couriers arrive.
Talk to store staff about what changes at dinner time. If too many orders arrive at once, try showing delivery promises based on how much the store can prepare.

Measure the share that arrives by the promised time. Also watch whether shoppers complete checkout and whether stores still earn enough per order. These extra measures are **guardrails**. They tell you if the change helps one part of the service while harming another.

blocks.value: Product lifecycle

A product lifecycle describes the kinds of work a team does as it turns an idea into something people use. Teams often revisit stages as they learn. Consider a bank building a feature that helps people set aside money for a goal.

value: **Discovery.** Talk with customers who want to save regularly. Learn where their current routine breaks down and how often it happens.
**Validation.** Sketch a savings-goal setup and watch customers try it. Check that they find it useful and easy to use, the bank can build it, and the cost makes sense.
**Delivery.** Build the feature and record events such as a goal being created or funded. A small trial with employees can expose problems before customers depend on it.
**Launch.** Release it to a small group, such as 5% of eligible customers. Prepare support staff and agree when to pause.
**Measurement.** Compare the share of customers who fund a goal with an earlier starting value or a suitable comparison group. Look at errors and support calls as well.
**Iteration.** Use those results to improve the setup, expand it, or roll it back.

blocks.value: The setup the team ships is the **output**. A higher share of customers creating and funding a goal is an **outcome**, a change that happened for people.
Systems thinking

Follow the chain of events beyond the screen. A **bottleneck** is the step that limits how much the whole service can handle. If a store can pack 20 orders an hour and couriers can carry 30, adding more couriers leaves the packing limit at 20. Check picking queues to see the problem as it starts.

A **delay** is the time between an action and its effect. A discount may raise checkout completion today and crowd the packing queue tonight. Customers who get late orders may wait weeks before you see fewer repeat purchases.

A **reinforcing loop** builds on itself. Reliable orders can build trust, bring customers back, and give the service more information to improve its estimates. A **balancing loop** pushes back as a limit is reached. More demand can overload the store, slow deliveries, and reduce future demand.

**Practice.** Orders are late after 6 p.m. Pick a group to study, name a timestamp that would help you locate the bottleneck, and suggest a test you could undo. **Hint.** Pair on-time delivery with a guardrail that might get worse.

glossary.definition: A measure that alerts you when a change is causing harm somewhere else. For example, watch checkout completion while testing more realistic delivery promises.
The step that limits how much work the whole process can handle. A slow packing station can hold up deliveries even when plenty of couriers are available.
Something the team creates or releases, such as a new savings screen.
A result for customers or the business, such as more customers actually putting money into a savings goal.
The work of finding a problem, testing an idea, building and launching it, then measuring and improving it.
A starting value you measure before a change. It helps you see how much a result moved afterward.
A cycle where an effect feeds back and makes the original change stronger. Reliable deliveries can bring more orders and better data for estimates.
A cycle that pushes back against a change. An overloaded store slows down, which can reduce how many orders people place later.

walkthrough.title: Find the bottleneck in a library pickup service
walkthrough.scenario: Harbor Library lets members reserve books online and collect them on Saturday mornings. People are waiting in line even after getting a “ready” message. The library director asks the team to build a pickup tracker. The product manager starts by finding out where the delay begins. All figures in this exercise are fictional.

blocks.value: Decide what the product manager should investigate

value: **Ask who is affected.** Talk with members who collect books during the Saturday rush. One member cannot wait more than 10 minutes before their bus leaves. That detail turns a general complaint into a service problem the team can measure.

**Follow actual orders.** Record when staff receive the request, find the book, place it on the pickup shelf, and hand it over. The handoff takes a minute. Staff spend most of their time finding reserved books after members arrive.

**Agree on the outcome.** Aim for more members to collect a complete reservation within 10 minutes. The PM and staff choose the measure together. A designer sketches clearer ready messages. An engineer checks that the shelf status can drive those messages. Library operations tests the new shelf routine.

blocks.value: Work through the product lifecycle

During discovery, the team learns that members trust a message labeled “ready.” To validate a different service, staff pre-sort books for one group and send the message only after all its books are on the shelf. This manual test can answer whether a ready message timed to real availability helps before the team invests in software.

For delivery, engineers connect the status message to the staff checklist. Launch the change at one branch so staff can manage exceptions. For measurement, compare similar Saturday windows and review missing-book complaints. If the outcome improves, continue testing and adjust the routine before expanding.

The new shelf workflow and status message are outputs. A higher share of members getting their books within 10 minutes is the outcome. Report the share alongside a guardrail for incomplete reservations, because a quick handoff is little help when a book is missing.
Follow the queue beyond the pickup screen

If 30 members arrive each hour and staff can prepare 20 reservations per hour, about 10 additional members are waiting by the end of each busy hour. Adding a second handoff desk changes little while the preparation step limits the service. Pre-sorting 15 reservations before opening could absorb some of the first-hour demand.

There is a delay between a bad pickup and a member deciding to stop reserving books. Monitor the queue while it forms and compare repeat reservations later. A reinforcing loop could start when reliable pickups make people trust the service and reserve again. When that creates more demand than staff can prepare, growing waits can slow demand again. This balancing loop is a reason to check capacity as the pilot grows.

practice.prompt: In a one-hour pilot, 42 people arrive. Staff prepare 28 reservations during the hour and have 10 complete reservations ready at opening. How many reservations can they fulfill at most, and what would you measure besides speed?
practice.answer: At most 38 reservations are available, from 28 prepared during the hour plus 10 ready in advance. At least four arrivals could still wait beyond that hour if each needs one reservation. Track the share of handoffs with every reserved book included.

walkthrough.interview: I first find the step that limits the customer outcome. Then I test a change at that step, measure the result customers experience, and watch a guardrail so the change does not create a different problem.

blocks.value: From a vision to a plan

A **vision** describes the future the product should help create. A grocery service might want busy families to get dinner on the table without worrying about when the ingredients will arrive. That gives the team a direction. It still needs to choose where to start.

value: **Make a strategy choice.** Focus first on families ordering evening groceries in neighborhoods the service can reach reliably. Invest in accurate stock and dependable delivery slots. Put expansion to more cities and a much larger catalog later.
**Choose an objective.** Aim to deliver a larger share of eligible evening orders by the time promised at checkout. The objective is the change the team wants to see.

**Set the roadmap.** Work on stock accuracy before offering narrower delivery windows. A narrow window is harder to keep when items go missing during preparation. The first project is a **dependency**, something the second project needs to work.

blocks.value: Review the roadmap when new evidence changes your understanding. If a small store trial shows that stock is accurate and pickup is the real source of delay, move pickup improvements earlier.
Connect the feature to a result

An **output** is what the team ships. A **product outcome** is what customers do or experience differently. A **business outcome** is what improves for the organization. Write a **hypothesis** that links the three so people can check the idea.

Suppose the business wants to earn more from repeat orders. You think a reorder button could help first-time buyers place a second order within 30 days. The button is the output. More second orders within 30 days is the product outcome. More money remaining after the variable costs of those orders is the business outcome.

Count only first-time buyers who have had the full 30 days to reorder. If 20 out of 100 eligible buyers reorder, the rate is 20%. Also measure refunds and contribution per order as guardrails. A promotion could bring people back and still cost more than it earns.
Compare ideas using RICE
To compare two ideas, use the same group, time period, and goal. RICE combines four estimates. Write down what supports each estimate so the team knows which numbers to question.

value: **Reach.** How many people or events would this affect in the period?
**Impact.** How much would it help each person you reach? Use the same scale for every idea.
**Confidence.** How sure are you about your estimates? Write 80% as 0.80 in the calculation.
**Effort.** How much time would the whole team need? Two people working full-time for a month each is two person-months.

blocks.value: **RICE score = reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort.**

Stock accuracy reaches 4,000 shoppers per quarter. With impact 1, confidence 80%, and effort 2 person-months, it scores 1,600. A new animation reaches 5,000 shoppers but has impact 0.25, confidence 80%, and effort 1. It scores 1,000. Higher reach alone did not win.
Ask which work you would delay to make room. A loyalty perk might depend on changes to billing or hurt margin. Weigh dependencies, fit with the strategy, and what could go wrong alongside the scores.

**Practice.** Write a sentence that links an idea to a customer outcome and a business result. Score two ideas with RICE, then pick one estimate to verify. **Hint.** Check whether the evidence supports the same impact scale for both ideas.

glossary.definition: The future you want the product to help create.
Choices about whom to serve, which need to focus on, and how to do it well.
The planned order of work and learning. The order can change when new evidence comes in.
Something that must be ready for another piece of work to succeed.
A change in what people do or experience, such as more first-time buyers ordering again.
A measurable result for the organization, such as earning more money from repeat orders after costs.
The revenue remaining after the variable costs you defined, such as picking, payment processing, and delivery.
A scoring method that uses reach, impact, confidence, and effort to compare ideas.
The value of work you give up or delay when you choose something else.

walkthrough.title: Decide which meal-ordering improvement to build first
walkthrough.scenario: Sprout Kitchen runs an after-school meal ordering app. Families like the food but often discover a meal is unavailable after they start placing an order. The team can either improve live availability or add colorful meal badges this quarter. These figures are fictional.

blocks.value: Turn a broad vision into a sequence

value: **Describe the future.** Sprout Kitchen wants families to be able to plan a school-night meal that they can actually collect.

**Choose who and where.** Start with families ordering for pickup at two kitchens, where staff can update the menu reliably. Expanding to all sites would spread the team across kitchens with different inventory systems.
**Set an outcome objective.** Raise the share of first-time buyers who place a second completed pickup order within 30 days, while keeping refunds and per-order contribution within agreed limits.

**Find the dependency.** Verify that staff can report sold-out dishes before changing what the app promises. The roadmap starts with the stock feed pilot, then adds live availability in checkout. A roadmap change is warranted if the pilot reveals that most failures come from payment instead.

blocks.value: Link a feature to customer and business results

Showing sold-out dishes before checkout is the output. The product hypothesis is that families can make a successful first order and will be more willing to come back. The business hypothesis is that the extra completed repeat orders will add contribution after variable costs.

Suppose 50 of 200 first-time buyers reorder within 30 days in the baseline group and 66 of 200 in a comparable pilot group. The rates are 25% and 33%, a difference of 8 percentage points. There are 16 additional repeat buyers in the pilot. If each added one order at $3 contribution, those orders represent $48 of contribution before the cost of building the feature. Check which buyers had the full 30 days and what else changed during the pilot before crediting the feature.
Compare the ideas on one RICE scale

Both ideas use eligible checkout customers reached in the same quarter. Estimate impact per reached customer on the same scale for the goal of more successful orders. Use 2 for high impact and 0.5 for low impact. Confidence of 80% goes into the calculation as 0.80. Effort includes product, design, engineering, and testing work.

value.caption: Fictional quarterly feature estimates

blocks.value: Live availability = 2,400 × 2 × 0.80 ÷ 3 = 1,280.

Consider live availability first because it directly addresses the observed checkout problem and has the higher score. A stock-feed estimate of five person-months would lower its score to 768, so verify effort before committing. If the feed is required for the app to make trustworthy pickup promises, explain that dependency even if you change the ordering.

practice.prompt: The pilot finds that only 1,500 eligible customers will see live availability during the quarter. With impact 2, confidence 80%, and effort three person-months, what is its new score? What would you check before choosing between the ideas?
practice.answer: The score is 1,500 × 2 × 0.80 ÷ 3 = 800, equal to meal badges. Verify the estimated reach, then compare evidence about which change addresses the missed orders and whether the stock feed is ready.

walkthrough.interview: I translate the vision into a choice of customer and an observable outcome. Then I use consistent RICE estimates to compare possible solutions and explain any dependencies or weak evidence that could change the decision.

blocks.value: Break a large result into smaller parts

A key performance indicator, or **KPI**, is a measure that tells you whether an important goal is moving in the right direction. A **KPI tree** puts that measure at the top and shows the smaller measures that help explain it. Think of each branch as a question you can investigate when the top number changes.

Start with monthly contribution from repeat orders. Contribution per order is the revenue assigned to that order minus the variable costs the business has defined, such as delivery and picking. Break the monthly total into how many repeat buyers ordered, how often they ordered, and how much each order contributed on average.

**Monthly repeat-order contribution = active repeat buyers × repeat orders per active repeat buyer × average contribution per repeat order.** With 1,000 buyers, 2 orders each, and $4 per order, the total is $8,000.

Use the same month and order definition for each factor. This formula gives a dollar total. To count profitable orders instead, count only orders with contribution above zero. When the total falls, look at all three branches. If repeat frequency stayed steady, fewer active buyers or lower contribution per order could explain the fall.
Separate the calculation from a theory

Some branches are true because of the arithmetic. Others are a **hypothesis** about what causes a result. Reliable deliveries might lead to more repeat orders, but prices or product availability might affect both. Label the link as a hypothesis and look for evidence before treating it as a cause.

A **leading indicator** moves early. For example, stores sending accurate stock data might give an early clue about the success of a delivery change. A **lagging indicator** takes longer to observe, such as total repeat-order contribution after the end of the month. A good early clue can help the team investigate, even before it knows the final result.

Keep a small record for each measure. Include the formula, which orders or people count, the time window, where the data comes from, who owns it, and a guardrail. For example, a plan to improve contribution by lowering delivery costs should also watch late orders and refunds.
Discover the problem while delivery continues

**Discovery** means learning which problem is worth solving and what might work. An interview helps you hear how customers work around a problem. Event data shows when it happens and helps estimate how many people are affected. A prototype, or quick version of an idea, lets you watch people try the experience before investing in the full build.

value: Talk to shoppers who need ingredients by a fixed time. Ask about the last order that did not arrive when they needed it, then look for timing and cancellation patterns.

Identify what could make the idea fail. If shoppers may misunderstand the booking choices, test a clickable prototype. If you need to learn whether stores can keep a narrow delivery promise, run a manual pilot in a few stores.

If the key question is whether store systems can send stock updates fast enough, ask engineers to do a short **technical spike**. Record what result would change your plan and revisit the assumption as work progresses.

blocks.value: **Practice.** Put one KPI at the top of a page. Add three branches and label each as a calculation or a cause you still need to test. Pick a small test for one cause and state what result would change your plan.

glossary.definition: A measure you use to track a result that matters to your goal.
A diagram that breaks a main measure into smaller measures and possible causes.
An early signal that a later outcome might change, such as fewer stock errors.
A result that takes time to show up, such as contribution from repeat orders at the end of the month.
A belief the plan depends on that you still need to check.
A short engineering investigation that answers a specific question about how something might work.
A small test in a real setting, such as offering scheduled delivery in two stores before expanding.

walkthrough.title: Investigate a drop in repeat ticket revenue
walkthrough.scenario: BridgeStage sells tickets for local performances. The team sees a drop in contribution from returning customers. The first reaction is to launch another discount, but the team needs to understand which part of the result changed before deciding what to test. The example uses fictional monthly data.

blocks.value: Build a tree you can calculate

value: **Define the top number.** Monthly contribution from repeat orders is the money left after the defined variable order costs, such as ticket processing and customer support. Count orders from customers with a previous completed purchase.

**Make the branches match the total.** Count distinct active repeat buyers. Divide repeat orders by those buyers to get average order frequency. Divide repeat-order contribution by the number of those orders to get average contribution per order.
**Compare the periods.** Make the same calculation for March and April using the same time zone, time window, and order rules. Exclude the same kinds of canceled orders in both periods.

blocks.value: Repeat-order contribution = active repeat buyers × repeat orders per buyer × average contribution per order.

value.caption: Fictional monthly KPI tree

blocks.value: The overall amount fell by $1,000. In this breakdown, the visible change is 100 fewer active repeat buyers. The average frequency and contribution per order remain the same. Averages can conceal different patterns by event type, so the next step is to check which returning buyers are missing.
Separate arithmetic from cause

“We had 100 fewer active repeat buyers” is an observation from the calculation. “People came back less because their preferred events sold out” is a hypothesis. Check whether the decline clusters around the venues where capacity was tight. Also look at event schedules and price changes, which might affect attendance in the same weeks.

Measure the share of browsing sessions that encounter a sold-out preferred event as a leading indicator. Monthly repeat contribution is lagging because the team learns the total after customers have had time to buy. Monitor cancellation rates and net contribution per order so the response does not encourage bookings the venue cannot fulfill.
Learn while delivery continues

Ask returning customers about the last occasion they wanted a ticket. Compare what they remember with the events actually available at the time. If customers struggled to discover alternatives, a clickable prototype can test whether they understand suggestions for nearby dates. A manual pilot can have one venue send real alternatives to a small group. If the idea depends on reliable availability data, run a short technical spike to check how quickly the feed reflects sold-out inventory.

Write down the decision that evidence will change. If shoppers already found alternatives but canceled because the total price was too high, the team would investigate pricing before investing in recommendations.

practice.prompt: In May, 700 repeat buyers order 2.4 times each at $5 contribution per order. Calculate the top KPI and say what that number tells you about the proposed availability feature.
practice.answer: The KPI is 700 × 2.4 × $5 = $8,400. Frequency increased in the breakdown. Check which buyers saw the pilot and compare their results with a credible comparison group to learn whether the suggestions caused the increase.

walkthrough.interview: I use the KPI tree to isolate which component changed. Then I write down possible causes separately and choose an interview, data check, prototype, or pilot that can change our decision.

blocks.value: Learn from people before building

Design thinking is a way to explore an uncertain problem. Stanford d.school describes five modes. Imagine you are helping older customers who have trouble ordering medicine online. Each mode gives you a different thing to learn or try.

value: **Empathize.** Watch a few customers place a typical order. Ask them to tell you about their last attempt. Observe where they hesitate, reread a label, or ask for help.
**Define.** Describe the difficulty you saw. For example, customers struggle to check the address and dosage before payment. That is more specific than saying the site needs to be easier.
**Ideate.** Generate several ways to solve that difficulty. Try bigger text, clearer labels, or a shorter review page. Leave time for different people to suggest options before choosing.
**Prototype.** Sketch one or two review pages on paper or make a simple screen the customer can click through.

**Test.** Give someone a realistic ordering task without coaching. Note which details they miss and whether they can correct a mistake. If they struggle earlier in the flow, go back and revise the problem.

blocks.value: **Divergent thinking** means opening up the options. **Convergent thinking** means narrowing those options with evidence and constraints, such as readability and the team's ability to ship a change safely. You may open up the options again when a test shows you missed something.
Who makes which decision?
Product management, project management, and product ownership overlap, but each role asks a different question. Consider a clinic preparing to release a new appointment-booking service.

value: A **product manager** asks what result the service should improve. If many patients abandon their first booking, the PM might prioritize the group struggling most and measure successful first bookings.

A **project manager** asks what work must happen, in what order, and who will do it. For the release, they might coordinate approval dates, staffing, training at the clinic, and the risk of missing a deadline.

A **Scrum Product Owner** is accountable for maximizing the value the Scrum Team creates and managing the **Product Backlog** effectively. The Product Owner communicates the Product Goal and keeps the list of work clear and ordered. They might place cancellation and rescheduling rules above a visual polish item because the rules are essential to the release.

blocks.value: Some teams combine the roles. One person may be both product manager and Product Owner. A useful planning meeting makes responsibility explicit. Ask who can change priorities, who checks whether the customer outcome improved, and who coordinates work that depends on another team.
Work through a last-minute request

A clinic asks to add another booking option one week before launch. The PM asks which patients need it and how it might affect completed bookings. The project manager checks what the extra work means for training, testing, and the release date. The Product Owner determines where it should sit in the backlog based on the Product Goal and existing work. Together, they can decide whether it belongs in this release or a later one.

**Practice.** The clinic also wants to change the reminder design. Who should decide whether this is valuable? Who checks whether the release still fits the schedule? Who orders it against other backlog items? **Hint.** Name a decision for each role.

glossary.definition: Observe and listen to learn what a person experiences in a real situation.
Generate different ways to address the same problem.
A quick model of an idea that lets you learn before building the complete product.
Explore more ideas or ways to describe a problem before narrowing the options.
Use evidence and constraints to decide which options deserve attention.
Scrum’s evolving, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.
A future state of the product that gives the Scrum Team a shared target.

walkthrough.title: Design a better way to reschedule a clinic visit
walkthrough.scenario: Sunbeam Clinic is preparing a new booking portal. Its front desk asks for a quick button to move appointments. Before launch, the team wants to understand why patients currently call and what a safe rescheduling experience would require. This is a fictional design exercise.

blocks.value: Learn what the patient is trying to do

value: **Empathize.** In a test, four of six participants say they want to know which other times exist before giving up the one they already have. They navigate back to their booking when they see a button labeled “Cancel.”
**Define.** Patients who need a different time hesitate because they cannot tell whether exploring alternatives will release their current slot.
**Ideate.** Widen the set of possibilities. Try a “See other times” preview, a request for the front desk to call, or a guided exchange with a confirmation page. This is divergent thinking.
**Prototype.** Sketch two screens showing the current appointment and optional replacement slots. Include the expected outcome if a replacement fills while the patient is deciding.

**Test.** Ask someone to move a fictional booking to next week. Watch whether they know which appointment they hold after previewing, confirming, or seeing an error. Narrow the options based on observed understanding and what can be built safely. This is convergent thinking.

blocks.value: Six sessions help reveal ways the design can fail. A larger trial with real appointment traffic can later estimate how often those problems occur. If people still misunderstand whether their old slot is safe, revisit the confirmation language before adding more booking options.
Give the roles different decisions to own

value.caption: Example decisions during the booking project
rows: Choose which patient problem matters most and measure successful self-service rescheduling.
Coordinate the front-desk training, testing, and release dependencies, and explain schedule effects.
Keep the Product Goal clear and order safe exchange behavior ahead of decorative work in the Product Backlog.

blocks.value: One person may hold multiple roles in a small team. Name the person responsible for each decision anyway so the group knows whom to ask when a deadline and a quality concern conflict.
Make a release decision from the evidence

A week before launch, an internal test reveals that clicking “change” can release the old slot before the replacement is confirmed. Losing an existing appointment is serious enough to pause release of self-service exchange. The PM checks how often people need to reschedule and identifies the main outcome. The project manager finds time for availability and concurrency tests. The Product Owner puts the safe exchange behavior ahead of the optional calendar theme.

The team can launch booking with a clearly labeled assisted reschedule path while validating the safer exchange. Measure completion time, repeat calls, and unexpected lost appointments during the pilot. An observed lost appointment would trigger an immediate review.

practice.prompt: A prototype lets the patient compare appointments, but two participants cannot tell whether their request succeeded after confirming. What would you test next, and which roles help decide how it fits into launch?
practice.answer: Test clearer confirmation that names the new date, time, and what happened to the previous booking. The PM checks whether understanding and successful completion improve, the project manager checks release timing and test coverage, and the Product Owner orders confirmation work against the other changes.

walkthrough.interview: I use design thinking to find the reason behind the requested feature and test the riskiest part of the experience. I make ownership explicit so customer outcomes, delivery risks, and backlog priorities each get a clear decision.

modules.title: Customers, opportunities, and research
modules.summary: Find the problem through customer jobs, interviews, and journey maps.

blocks.value: Find the progress the customer wants

A **job-to-be-done**, or JTBD, describes what a person is trying to accomplish in a situation. Think of the product as something they might use to get that job done. They may also choose an existing habit or a workaround, such as doing the task by hand. The job stays the same even when their chosen solution changes.

Imagine a parent whose workday ends late. The family needs dinner soon, and the parent has little time to compare menus. Their job might be to get a dependable meal on the table with little planning. They could order delivery, heat leftovers, pick up takeaway, or stop at a nearby shop. A grocery app competes with all of those choices. A smaller list of meals with reliable arrival times might help more than a huge catalog.

value: Name the **situation** that starts the job, such as finishing work after 6 p.m. on a weekday.
Describe the **motivation**, such as wanting to feed the family without another time-consuming decision.
State the **desired progress**, such as having a dinner everyone can eat on the table by 7 p.m.

blocks.value: Ask about the last time this happened. What did they try first? What did they rule out? What made the final choice feel safe? Answers about recent behavior help you understand why a person changes their routine or sticks with it.
Group people when it changes a decision

A **segment** is a group whose needs, behavior, circumstances, or cost to serve justify a different decision. The person who pays can be different from the person who uses the service. An office manager may pay for a team lunch and need one receipt. The employees who eat it may care about dietary labels and portion sizes. Check both groups when planning the service.

For grocery orders, compare shoppers who plan a week ahead with those who need ingredients tonight. The first group may want to choose what can be substituted when a product is out of stock. The second group may care more about a dependable arrival time. Check real orders, interviews, and support records to see if the two groups actually behave differently. Then ask how you could identify and reach each group and whether serving them differently is worth the effort.
Use personas as short research summaries

A **persona** is a short description of a recurring pattern in your research. It should help someone remember a user's goal, situation, behavior, and barriers. Include a link or note pointing to the evidence. Leave out personal details that would have no effect on a decision.

“Ravi, the shift worker” could represent customers who order regularly after midnight. The useful details are the late hours, limited availability, and need for accurate restaurant opening times. If enough research supports it, test whether showing only restaurants that can fulfill the order reduces late-night cancellations. If other late-night customers plan orders in advance, revise or split the persona to reflect that difference.

**Practice.** Choose a service you used last week. Write one job in the form “When ___, I want ___, so I can ___.” Then name a segment that encounters the job and one observation a persona could use. **Hint.** Your job should make sense even if the app disappeared.

glossary.definition: A way to describe the progress a person wants in a particular situation, regardless of which product they use.
A different way of doing something when the usual route is inconvenient or fails. Heating leftovers can solve the dinner problem without ordering.
A group of people whose shared needs or behavior justify making a different product or marketing decision.
The person or organization who buys the product. The people who use it may be different.
A short, research-backed description of a recurring user pattern. It helps a team remember what matters when making decisions.
A replacement item used when the product someone ordered is unavailable.

walkthrough.title: Find the job behind a shared laundry booking
walkthrough.scenario: Alder Apartments has six washing machines and a booking app. The building manager wants residents to use it more. Residents already find ways to wash clothes, including borrowing a machine from a friend and going to a laundromat. The team studies when those choices make sense. All examples and counts are fictional.

blocks.value: Start with the last time someone needed the service

value: **Find the trigger.** Ask a resident to describe their last load from start to finish. One resident noticed they were out of clean work clothes at 7 p.m. after their shift changed.

**Ask about the alternatives.** They checked for a free machine, walked down to see if it worked, then took the load to a nearby laundromat. Ask what made the extra trip worthwhile. The answer was knowing they would finish before bed.

**Write the job in their words.** “When I get home late and need clothes for tomorrow, I want a dependable way to finish one load tonight so I can get ready for work.” The job describes the progress that would still matter if the booking app disappeared.

blocks.value: Group people by decisions you can make differently

Some residents book laundry every Sunday. They plan ahead and would value a recurring slot or a simple way to release it. Others wash whenever a shift ends. For them, seeing the earliest working machine matters more than recurring reservations. A single “uses the laundry room” segment would hide this difference.

In a small study, nine of 12 planned bookings were created at least a day ahead. Seven of 10 short-notice users had tried a machine in the previous hour. This evidence suggests two situations worth testing. Before estimating their size, check whether the log records walk-ins and machine faults as consistently as app bookings.

The manager pays for the booking system and wants fewer disputes. Residents use the system and want clean clothes at a predictable time. Ask both groups what would count as improvement. For example, a change that reduces calls by removing a support button might leave residents stranded.
Build a persona around evidence

Call the short-notice pattern “the after-shift washer.” Record the situation, desired result, current workaround, and what creates uncertainty. Link those details to the interview or observation that supports them. Someone's age and favorite hobbies belong in the summary only if they affect the decision.

Try a card showing the next verified working slot in one building. Measure the share of residents who start a short-notice booking and complete a load within two hours. Also track wrong availability messages and queue conflicts. Split the persona if some residents want immediate access while others need assurance that their later slot will still be free.

practice.prompt: A resident says “Please add push notifications.” How would you turn the request into a job and decide which group to investigate?
practice.answer: Ask what happened the last time they missed a laundry slot and what they did next. A possible job is “When my plans change, I want to know whether my reserved machine is still available so I can finish the load today.” Compare residents with firm schedules and residents whose shifts change before choosing an alert or a flexible booking option.

walkthrough.interview: I write the job around the progress a person wants in a specific situation. I use segments and personas when evidence shows that the same product decision will help those situations differently.

blocks.value: Draw the experience as it happens today

A **customer journey map** follows one group of people through a specific situation. It starts when a need comes up, which may be before anyone opens an app. It can end after the order arrives, or after support resolves a problem. Map the current experience first so a redesign responds to real gaps.

value: Choose a situation, such as an office manager ordering lunch for eight people before a meeting.
List stages in order. They notice the need, choose a restaurant, check the arrival time, pay, track the order, and receive it. Add what happens if an item is missing.

At each stage, record what the buyer does, what question they have, and any **friction**, or difficulty. Someone checking the arrival time may wonder whether the food will be there before the meeting.

Add the work happening **backstage**. The restaurant prepares the food, a courier accepts the delivery, and support handles missing items. A grocery item removed during picking may appear to the customer as a surprise at the door.

blocks.value: Check the map against customer interviews, event timestamps, and operations records. If they disagree, mark the uncertain stage so the team can learn more before designing a new experience.
Turn observations into an insight

An **observation** describes what you saw. An **insight** is an explanation of what that pattern may mean. Start with the evidence, look for a recurring pattern, suggest a cause, and state how you could check it. Look for people whose behavior does not fit your explanation.

Imagine order data shows that customers reopen tracking three or four times in ten minutes. Several customers tell you they cannot tell whether the restaurant started preparing the order. That suggests they check because the time estimate feels untrustworthy. Missing notifications and urgent orders are other plausible reasons. Compare notification records and the same behavior on less urgent orders before you choose what to change.
Compare problems you could address

An **opportunity** is a problem or need that, if addressed, could improve a result. Ask how often it happens, how serious it is, which group it affects, whether it fits the strategy, and how much the team could realistically help.

value: Interviews give context about what happened and why a person chose an alternative.
A survey sent to a suitable sample can help estimate how many people face the issue.
Support tickets show recurring problems among people who contacted support.
Funnel data shows where people stop progressing, while a review of competing services shows what else they could use.

blocks.value: Teresa Torres’s **opportunity-solution tree** connects a desired result to customer needs, possible ways to help, and small tests. Suppose you want fewer abandoned grocery orders. Some shoppers may leave when they first see the delivery fee at payment. Others understand the fee but decide it costs too much. The first group might need an earlier estimate. The second might value a different bundle or service level. Compare interview themes with checkout data before picking a test.

**Practice.** Turn one complaint into an observation, possible insight, and opportunity. Name another explanation and what evidence would separate it from yours. **Hint.** “People reopened tracking” describes a behavior. “They did not trust the estimate” still needs evidence.

glossary.definition: A picture of the stages someone goes through while trying to get something done, from the first trigger to the end.
Something that makes a task harder, slower, or more confusing.
Work the customer cannot see, such as a restaurant preparing food or a system assigning a courier.
A description of what happened that you can point to in the evidence.
A supported interpretation of why a pattern matters. It may still need testing.
A customer problem or unmet need that could improve a desired result if addressed.
A diagram linking a desired result to customer needs, possible solutions, and ways to test them.

walkthrough.title: Trace where a team lunch order goes wrong
walkthrough.scenario: Pine Lunch lets office coordinators order meals for meetings. Coordinators reopen order tracking while the food is on its way. A designer proposes a live map. The team traces the order first so it can tell whether location is the problem. All figures are fictional.

blocks.value: Map the experience and the backstage work

value: **Set the boundary.** Follow a coordinator ordering lunch for eight people before a 12:30 meeting. Start when the calendar invite appears and finish after everyone has a meal or support has resolved any missing items.
**Write actions and questions.** At each stage, record what the coordinator does, what they need to know, and what makes it hard. Keep notes from sessions and logs next to the stage they describe.

**Add the backstage events.** Check when the restaurant accepts, when it marks the order as packed, when a courier picks it up, and when support hears about a problem. Mark timestamps you do not yet trust.

value.caption: A section of the current-state journey
rows: Can this restaurant handle eight meals by noon?
Is noon still the promised time?
Did the restaurant actually accept the order?
Can I replace a missing meal in time?

blocks.value: Test what the observation might mean

In 60 group orders, 18 coordinators opened tracking at least three times in ten minutes. Five of eight interviewees described checking while the app still said “Order received.” The observation is repeated checking. One possible insight is that coordinators cannot tell if the restaurant committed to prepare the order. Urgent meetings or missed notifications could also explain the behavior.

Check whether repeat opens are more common in orders with long acknowledgment delays. Separate urgent orders from orders with an ample delivery window, then verify whether notifications were delivered. If customers mainly return after a failed notification, start with alert reliability. If checking clusters before acceptance even when notifications work, a trustworthy acceptance status is a better candidate.
Compare opportunities before picking a solution

Put “more complete team orders by the promised time” at the top of an opportunity-solution tree. Two opportunities are helping coordinators know whether a restaurant has accepted and helping them recover quickly from missing meals. Their evidence is different. Tracking logs and interviews inform acceptance visibility, while support records and item checks can reveal missing meals. A survey of recent group-order buyers can estimate how often each need occurs, including people who never contacted support.

An acceptance label and a backup restaurant option are solutions to explore. First test whether people can interpret an accurate acknowledgment with a simple prototype. If acknowledgment arrives too late to change behavior, investigate restaurant operations before investing in the label.

practice.prompt: Many buyers open tracking frequently, but almost all affected orders are scheduled within 25 minutes of the meeting. What would you compare before deciding to build a status feature?
practice.answer: Compare similarly urgent orders with short and long acknowledgment delays. Look for repeat opens after acknowledgment and after missed alerts. If urgency explains checking across both groups, learn whether buyers want a more realistic ordering cutoff or another way to plan a backup.

walkthrough.interview: I map real actions and backstage events, then separate what happened from why it might have happened. That lets me test the customer need before committing to the most obvious feature.

blocks.value: Connect work to the change you want

**Impact mapping** is a way to connect a measurable goal to the people who can affect it, their possible behavior changes, and the work that may help. Gojko Adzic's framework uses four questions. Start with the goal so the team can compare features by the result they might help produce.

value: **Why?** A clinic wants to reduce missed appointments from 12% to 9% next quarter.
**Who?** Patients who sometimes need to change their booking and clinic staff who manage open times can influence that result. In the map, these people are called **actors**.
**How?** Patients could confirm or reschedule earlier. Staff could reopen canceled slots so other patients can book them.
**What?** Test a one-tap confirmation or rescheduling link and a queue that helps staff see which slots to reopen.

blocks.value: Every connection is a proposed explanation you can check. First measure whether patients confirm or reschedule earlier and whether staff release more slots. Then check whether missed appointments fall. If confirmations rise and attendance stays the same, look for reasons patients still cannot attend. You might need a different behavior change before you need a better reminder design.
Plan user research in five steps

Imagine customers often stop when a service asks them to verify their identity. User research can help you tell whether the issue comes from unclear instructions, inaccessible controls, or trouble taking a usable photo. Pick a method based on what you need to learn.

value: **Define the decision and question.** Decide what choice the study will inform. Ask which step is hard to finish, for whom, and under what conditions.

**Choose a method and sample.** Interviews explain people's motivations and workarounds. A usability session lets you watch them try the task. Analytics helps locate the step or estimate how often it blocks progress. Include recent abandoners and people who completed verification. Recruit across the relevant devices and access needs.
**Prepare neutral prompts.** Try “Walk me through the last time you tried to verify your identity.” Ask what the person saw and did. Avoid wording that suggests which answer you expect.

**Run and record the sessions.** Explain what will happen and get informed consent. Make the session accessible. Use dummy documents or a properly protected test setting so people can participate without exposing sensitive information. Write down what they did separately from what you think it means.

**Synthesize the findings.** Group repeated problems, note exceptions, and compare them with the funnel data. If several participants misread the photo instructions, check how many actual customers exit at that step. Share what you found, where the evidence is limited, and what decision it supports.

blocks.value: Keep the research question focused. “How can we fix verification?” is broad. “What stops first-time customers on mobile from submitting a readable photo?” gives you a group, a setting, and an action to observe.

**Practice.** Write a research question about shoppers who stop checkout when a delivery fee appears. Decide whom to recruit, what you would watch, and which data could show how common it is. **Hint.** Include people who saw the fee and continued, too.

glossary.definition: A diagram that links a measurable goal to the people, behavior changes, and work that may help achieve it.
A person or group who can influence the goal in an impact map, such as clinic staff.
The group of people included in a study. Who you include affects which conclusions you can draw.
A study where you watch someone try a realistic task to see what helps or blocks them.
A question that gives someone room to answer without suggesting the answer you want.
A participant's agreement after you explain what the research involves and what will happen to their information.
The work of grouping and comparing evidence to find patterns, exceptions, and implications.

walkthrough.title: Reduce missed sessions at a community workshop
walkthrough.scenario: The Cedar Workshop offers free equipment training by reservation. Empty seats waste staff time and leave people on the waitlist. The team has one month to test a change. Its starting records show 18 missed sessions out of 150 reservations still held at start time, a fictional rate of 12%.

blocks.value: Connect proposed work to a measurable goal

value: **Why?** Aim to reduce missed reservations from 12% to 9% next quarter. Count a reservation as missed when it is still held at the session start and the attendee does not come.
**Who?** Attendees who need to change plans can release reservations. Front-desk staff can offer released seats to waitlisted people. Both are actors because their actions can affect the goal.
**How?** Help attendees release seats early enough for staff to refill them. Help staff identify the next person to offer a seat. These are changes in behavior you can observe.
**What?** Try a reminder with a release link and a simple waitlist queue. Each idea supports one behavior. Test the behavior before deciding whether the idea needs more features.

blocks.value: Watch actual attendance and refilled seats alongside the missed rate. More people could release their reservations on time and still leave seats empty. If reminders increase confirmations but attendance remains flat, interview people who confirmed and still could not attend. Timing or transport might require a different approach.
Plan research around the decision

value: **Define the decision.** Ask whether the next test should make it easier for attendees to release a reservation or for staff to refill it. A focused question is “What prevents people from releasing a seat at least two hours before the start?”

**Choose methods and people.** Talk with people who attended, released early, and missed their last session. Include users with different devices and access needs. Use analytics to estimate how often early releases happen and a usability session to see whether someone can use the link.
**Write neutral prompts.** Ask “When did you realize you could not come?” and “What did you do next?” Let them show the steps on a sample booking.

**Run and record responsibly.** Explain the exercise, get consent, and use dummy reservations. Record what participants do separately from your explanation. Give participants access accommodations and a way to stop.
**Synthesize and recommend.** Group recurring blockers, include exceptions, and compare what people say with observed release timestamps. Share the sample limits and the decision the results support.

blocks.value: Read the result alongside the behavior

Suppose 8 of 10 usability participants release a sample seat without help, but in a live pilot only 3 of 12 released seats are refilled. The first result suggests the link is understandable in the session. The second points to a separate handoff problem. Check time from release to staff offer and whether waitlisted people can accept in time. The queue may deserve the next test even if the link still needs improvement.

practice.prompt: Confirmations increase from 60% to 78% after a reminder test. Missed reservations and attendance are unchanged. What part of the map would you revise?
practice.answer: The reminder changed confirmation behavior. The link from confirmation to attendance still needs evidence. Ask why confirmed participants still miss sessions and consider an earlier release or reschedule option. Keep tracking attendance so the team can see whether the new behavior helps the goal.

walkthrough.interview: I map a measurable goal to the actors who can influence it, the behaviors we need, and ideas that could help. I test the behavior and the outcome so we can see where our reasoning breaks down.

lessons.title: From customer evidence to a testable problem

blocks.value: Ask questions that produce useful evidence

An **interview** helps you learn what happened, what mattered to the customer, and what they did next. Recruit people with recent experience of the situation. If you study changing delivery estimates, talk to people who kept the order as well as people who canceled it. Hearing both stories helps you avoid assuming everyone reacts the same way.

Ask someone to walk through their last order. “When did you see the new time?” can lead to “What did you do next?” Asking “Would you like live tracking?” steers people toward your idea and asks them to guess what they would do. An actual experience gives you details you can compare with order records.

Use a **survey** to estimate how common a pattern is. Ask about a clear time window, such as the past 30 days, and include choices for people who did not order or cannot remember. Test the wording with a few people first. A survey sent only to people who complained tells you about that group. Note who was invited and who answered before applying the result to all customers.
Define the problem before naming a feature
A **problem statement** describes the customer, their situation, what they need, and what happens if the need is unmet. Separate the facts you observed from the parts you still need to check.

For example, first-time grocery shoppers ordering after work need to know if groceries will arrive before dinner. If the estimate changes after payment, some cancel and make another plan. Ask “How might we help first-time shoppers choose a delivery window they can rely on?” This leaves room to improve the estimate, show availability earlier, or make it easier to change the slot.
Turn the idea into a hypothesis you can test

A **hypothesis** states what you will change, what result you expect, and why. For example, showing a realistic delivery range before payment will reduce cancellations among first-time peak-hour orders because shoppers can choose a time that works for them.

value: Pick the riskiest assumption. If you do not know whether people understand the range, watch a few shoppers try a prototype. If you understand the screen but need to measure actual cancellations, use a controlled rollout with a suitable comparison group.

Write a test plan before starting. Define who qualifies, how long you will observe them, what you will measure, and what would count as success. An illustrative decision rule might require a fall from 10% to 9% in first-order cancellations, with acceptable checkout completion and support contacts.

Use enough observations to distinguish a useful improvement from ordinary changes. If the comparison is too uncertain, record that and decide what extra evidence or smaller test would help. A single busy weekend can move the rate without any change to the product.

blocks.value: **Practice.** Rewrite “We need live tracking” as a customer problem and a testable hypothesis. Name one primary metric and one guardrail. **Hint.** A move from 10% to 9% is a drop of one percentage point.

glossary.definition: A short description of who faces a difficulty, when it happens, what they need, and why it matters.
A prediction you can test about what a change will do and why.
A quick version of an idea that helps you learn before building the full product.
A small release that compares people seeing a change with a suitable group that does not see it.
The main number you use to judge whether the test achieved its goal.
A measure of a downside you want to limit, such as a rise in support calls.
The simple difference between two percentages. A change from 10% to 9% is a fall of one percentage point.

walkthrough.title: Turn a rental cancellation complaint into a fair test
walkthrough.scenario: Wren Gear rents camping equipment. Some first-time renters cancel after their pickup time changes. A teammate proposes live tracking. The product team first learns what makes people cancel and defines a result it can measure. The scenario uses fictional data.

blocks.value: Gather evidence from behavior

Interview people who canceled and people who kept a rental after a pickup change. Ask them to describe the last booking, when they saw the update, what else they had planned, and what they did next. One person had already booked a ride and changed stores when the new time appeared. Another kept their booking because they had a flexible afternoon. Comparing both helps identify the constraint.

Use a short survey to check how common the pattern is among recent eligible renters. Ask “In the past 30 days, did a pickup time change after you booked?” Provide choices for no rental, no change, and unsure. Check wording with a few people first. Report how many people answered and who was invited. Responses from cancellation complaints alone cannot describe all bookings.
Define the problem and preserve alternatives

A possible problem statement is “First-time renters collecting gear after work need a pickup time they can plan around. A change after booking can make their ride or store visit impractical, so some cancel.” Evidence so far is that customers describe schedule conflicts. How often a more accurate time would prevent cancellation remains open.

Frame an opportunity as “How might we help first-time renters choose a pickup window they can make?” Possibilities include showing a dependable range before checkout, offering another location, or allowing a quick change after booking. Each assumes a different cause of the problem.
Write the hypothesis and the rules before the test

value: **Name the change and reason.** “If we show a realistic pickup range before payment, fewer first-time renters will cancel after booking because they can choose a window that fits their plans.”

**Choose the smallest useful test.** Use a prototype first if you need to see whether customers interpret the range correctly. Once they understand it, compare the existing experience and the new range with eligible customers assigned consistently.

**Define success and harm.** Divide eligible bookings canceled within seven days of placement by all eligible bookings placed, including those later canceled. Give every booking a full seven days of observation. Also monitor checkout completion among eligible people who started checkout and support contacts. A drop in bookings could make the remaining group look better while the service gets harder to use.

**Set a decision rule.** For illustration, seek a drop from 12% to 9% cancellation with checkout completion no more than one percentage point lower and no increase in pickup disputes. Set the sample size and follow-up window before the test.

blocks.value: If 24 of 200 eligible bookings cancel in control and 18 of 200 cancel with the new range, the observed drop is 3 percentage points. Decide whether the difference is precise enough to act on, and check guardrails. One period with unusual store hours could change the result.

practice.prompt: Cancellation falls from 12% to 9%, but checkout completion falls from 70% to 66%. Would you expand the change under the stated rule?
practice.answer: Hold the rollout. The four-percentage-point drop breaches the checkout guardrail. Check which renters saw the widest windows and whether they left because a useful time was unavailable or because the new display was confusing.

walkthrough.interview: I use recent behavior to turn a feature request into a customer problem. Then I state what we will change, why it should help, and which outcome and guardrails will tell us whether to expand.

modules.title: Ideation, design, and delivery
modules.summary: Generate options, prototype an experience, and write testable requirements.

blocks.value: Make several choices before picking one

**Ideation** means coming up with different ways to help with a problem. Begin with a focused opportunity and some evidence. “Help patients reschedule when their work plans change” gives the team more to work with than “improve appointments.” Have people suggest ideas individually before the group evaluates them. This gives quieter team members time to think and makes it easier to see beyond the first proposal.

Try **brainwriting**. Each person writes several ideas, then reads the others and adds to them. Try an **analogy** by borrowing a useful pattern from another service, such as using a parcel-tracking timeline to show how far along a grocery order is. Change a constraint by asking how you would help if push notifications were unavailable, or if you could change the delivery process itself.

Suppose a clinic wants fewer missed appointments. Different ideas address different reasons for missing one. Adding a booking to a calendar may help someone who forgets. Easier rescheduling helps someone whose plans change. A waitlist can help the clinic fill a slot that opens up. A phone call might make sense for an appointment where missing it would be especially harmful. Group the ideas by need before comparing them.
Use a framework when the group gets stuck

Start by writing the goal, evidence, and need. Agree on what a solution must do well. For a grocery delivery estimate, it should be honest, arrive when the shopper needs it, and show a clear next step. These principles help you judge ideas after generating them.

value: **SCAMPER** is a list of prompts for changing something that already exists. Substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, or rearrange and reverse. For example, combine the estimated arrival time with a link to change the slot, or eliminate a checkout step that asks for the same information twice.

**Crazy 8s** gives each person eight minutes to sketch eight distinct ideas. A rough drawing is enough to show the difference between ideas. Afterward, select a few to explore and write down what you still need to learn.

blocks.value: Compare ideas on customer value, how easy they are to use, whether your team can build and operate them, and how they fit the strategy. For unreliable grocery estimates, compare showing prep status, giving a time range, and offering a later slot before payment. Ask which could solve the observed issue, how much work it needs, and how easily you could undo it if it causes harm.
Use a mind map to find questions

Put a topic such as late delivery in the center. Draw branches for stores, couriers, customers, and support. Add possible causes such as packing queues, courier availability, distance, weather, address errors, or carrying several orders together. Add opportunities and things you need to check on their own branches.

Convert a possible cause into a question. For example, are orders grouped together more likely to arrive late during the evening rush in one area? Compare relevant timestamps and ask couriers what happens there. The map helps the team see what to investigate. Use evidence to decide which branches deserve time.

**Practice.** Pick one cause of a missed appointment and sketch three ways to address it. Choose the smallest test you could run this week, then name the evidence that would make you choose a different idea.

glossary.definition: Generating several possible ways to solve the same problem.
A group technique where people write ideas on their own, then read and build on each other's ideas.
A comparison that helps you borrow a useful pattern from a different setting.
A limit that affects which ideas can work, such as time, cost, or which devices people can use.
Seven prompts for changing an existing idea. Combining two steps or removing one are two examples.
A timed activity where each person sketches eight different ideas in eight minutes.
Whether the team can build and run the idea with the resources and time it has.
A diagram with a topic in the center and related people, causes, ideas, or questions branching out.

walkthrough.title: Generate options for full bike-return stations
walkthrough.scenario: CitySpin rents bikes by the hour. At the end of a ride, some riders reach a full return station and have to find another one. The team has one week to learn which idea helps before deciding what to build. The scenario and numbers are fictional.

blocks.value: Generate several ways to help before scoring them

value: **Start with evidence.** Of 80 rides ending near the train station one evening, 18 riders tried to return a bike at a full station. Several told support they could not risk missing their train.

**Name the opportunity.** Help riders finish near the train station without an unexpected detour. Write what a solution must do well, such as offer accurate information in time to change course and leave a clear recovery path.

**Brainwrite before discussing.** Ask each of four teammates to write three ideas independently. Review the 12 suggestions together and build on them. Group them by the need they address, such as knowing whether a return will work, finding another station, or making space available.

**Borrow an analogy and vary a constraint.** Think about how parking garages show open spaces before a driver enters. Then imagine the bike app cannot send alerts. Could a sign, a better route on the map, or moving bikes at peak time help?

blocks.value: Use structured prompts and compare the options

With SCAMPER, start from the current “Station full” message. Substitute a walking-time estimate for the word “nearby.” Combine the warning and the directions to a station with space. Rearrange the sequence so the warning appears before the rider chooses a destination. Other prompts are adapt, modify, use a feature in another situation, and eliminate a step.

For Crazy 8s, give each person eight minutes to sketch eight distinct return ideas. A rough screen with one action is enough to show how an idea works. Pick a few sketches to investigate and name what remains uncertain.

value.caption: Compare ideas for the same return problem
rows: Show spare docks at route planning
Helps before the rider commits to a destination
How quickly does the count become stale?
Show the nearest station with space
Helps a rider recover at the destination
Can the rider understand the detour while stopped?
Move bikes out of crowded stations before peak
Can operations do this at a workable cost?

blocks.value: Turn a mind map into evidence

Put “failed bike return” at the center. Branch to riders, stations, app data, and operations. Under stations, list broken docks and stations that fill after a train arrives. Under app data, list delayed counts. Turn each branch into a question you could investigate. For example, do full-station reports rise after trains arrive even when the app count is current?

For a first test, have one operator check dock counts by hand during the rush and put verified alternatives in a route prototype. See whether riders can select an acceptable return location. If counts are accurate but every nearby station fills, test a capacity change before expanding the map.

practice.prompt: You have time for one field observation. Riders say the map is wrong, and staff say the station simply fills quickly. What evidence would help choose between these explanations?
practice.answer: Record the station's actual free docks and the app's displayed count at the same minute for several arrivals. Also note how rapidly docks fill. A persistent difference points to the feed. A matching count followed by rapid filling suggests the prediction or capacity needs attention.

walkthrough.interview: I separate idea generation from selection, then compare different ways to address the same need. I choose a small test based on the uncertainty that would most change the decision.

lessons.title: Designing the experience before building it

blocks.value: Make the important things easy to find

Good design helps someone see what matters, understand what actions are available, and recover when something goes wrong. **Visual hierarchy** is the order in which a design draws attention. A grocery checkout should make the total easy to find while still showing the subtotal, delivery fee, tax, and discount.

Align amounts so shoppers can compare them, and use space to show which numbers belong together. Choose readable type, clear contrast between text and background, and familiar button styles. “Place order” describes what happens if you press it. A button is an **affordance**, something the customer can act on, and its shape and label signal the action.

**Feedback** tells the shopper what happened. After payment, confirm the order. If payment fails, explain what they can try and keep the cart intact. Allow people to use the keyboard and see where focus is. Make touch controls large enough to use. Pair color with words or icons so people can understand an error even if they cannot distinguish the colors.
Sketch the screens with a wireframe

A **wireframe** is a rough sketch that shows what information and controls go on each screen. You can make one on paper. Use it to agree on the order of information and actions before spending time on colors, styling, or engineering.

Sketch an appointment-booking page with the provider, date, available times, and a confirmation screen. Add an option to reschedule. Include a “No times available” state and write down when the system should reserve a slot. Ask someone to book an appointment with the sketch and see whether they know what to do when no time fits.
Draw the paths people can take

A **user flow** describes how someone moves from a starting point to a finished task. Put actions and choices in order. Include paths for both success and recovery, since those often cross more than one screen.

value: For grocery reorder, start when a shopper opens a past order. Let them edit unavailable items and confirm whether they accept replacements.
Let the shopper pick a delivery time and pay. If they have no saved card, give them a way to add one without losing their cart.
If no delivery time is available, let them save the cart or choose another day. End the successful path with an order confirmation.

blocks.value: Walk through each branch to find places where a person has to repeat work or has no way forward.
Build only enough to test the question

A **prototype** imitates part of an experience. A paper prototype can test whether people know where to start. A clickable version can show whether they understand what a button does. A small technical prototype can show whether two systems can exchange information fast enough.

If you are testing a subscription pause, ask the customer to skip one month. Observe whether they can tell a pause from a cancellation and predict when they will next be billed. Explain which parts are simulated, such as payment and notifications. Add detail where it helps you answer the question.

**Practice.** Sketch a checkout with a successful payment and a failed payment. Follow both paths with a keyboard or on a phone. Check whether the customer can see the total, understand what happened, and recover without losing the order.

glossary.definition: The way size, placement, and emphasis guide your eyes to what matters first.
How clearly two things differ, such as dark text against a light background.
An action something makes possible. A button gives you something to press, and its label tells you what the press does.
A visible or audible response that tells you what happened after an action.
The control that will respond when you press a key. A visible outline can help you find it.
A rough picture of a screen showing what goes where.
A map of the actions and decisions a person goes through to finish a task.
A test version that imitates enough of a product to answer a specific question.

walkthrough.title: Sketch a room booking with a clear recovery path
walkthrough.scenario: Maple Center lets residents reserve community rooms. A resident wants a room for six people at 4 p.m. on Tuesday. Their preferred room may become unavailable while they are deciding. The team sketches the experience and tests what people understand before connecting live scheduling. This is a fictional example.

blocks.value: Make choices and feedback easy to see

Put the date, time, room capacity, and final action in a clear visual order. A heading such as “Choose a room for Tuesday” tells people where they are. Label available controls with actions such as “Select 4 p.m.” Use the usual button shape and styling so the control looks clickable. If a room is unavailable, state the reason and show another action, such as “See 4:30 p.m. rooms.”

When someone confirms, display the room, date, and time and explain where to find the booking. If a request fails, keep the choices and say what to try. In the prototype, check keyboard focus order, visible focus, and readable labels. Use words or icons alongside color so the error still makes sense to someone who cannot distinguish the colors.
Wireframe the few screens needed for the task

value: **Choose.** Sketch one screen with date, start time, room capacity, and alternatives. Give the task details more space than promotional content.

**Review.** Keep the chosen room, time, and any booking limit together, with clear “Change” and “Confirm reservation” actions. Write down when the app should hold a slot. In this test, selection shows availability, and confirmation checks it again.
**Confirm or recover.** Sketch a success message and an unavailable state. Keep the date, party size, and selected time visible when the user tries an alternative.
**Manage later.** Show where to find a confirmed booking and how to change it. This can be a rough panel if rescheduling is outside the current test.

blocks.value: Draw the path, then build just enough to test it

A user flow links actions and decisions across screens. The happy path is choose date → select room → review → confirm → see booking. One recovery path is choose date → select room → review → slot fills → see alternatives → choose a replacement → confirm. Another is a request timeout. Show a pending state and a way to check the booking before trying again, so the person knows whether to submit again.

Use paper to test whether participants can find the room choices. Use a clickable prototype to see whether they understand confirmation and can recover when the slot is taken. Tell them the booking is simulated. Use a small technical test if the remaining question is whether two users can safely request the final slot at the same time.

Ask a participant to book a room and then handle an unavailable slot without coaching. Record whether they can state what they booked and whether they repeat steps. If they lose the date or party size, fix recovery and test again before refining the color palette.

practice.prompt: In a usability session, the participant presses Confirm again after a slow response. What design and technical questions should you test?
practice.answer: Show a pending status with a clear way to check the result. Test whether users understand that their request is in progress. Separately, test whether repeated submissions are treated as one booking and the final status is reliable.

walkthrough.interview: I use a wireframe to agree on what belongs on a screen and a flow to check what happens between screens. Then I prototype the smallest part that can answer the usability or technical question.

blocks.value: Write down what needs to work

A **product requirements document** (PRD) gives the team one place to see why a change matters, what the release must do, and how to judge whether it works. Start with the user problem and the evidence. Name who is affected, the change you want to see, and how you will measure it. Make the **scope** clear by listing what this release covers and what it leaves for later.

Suppose customers abandon checkout when the delivery fee appears late. The team plans to show a clear price breakdown. The PRD should say where the subtotal, fee, tax, and discounts appear. Explain when an estimate becomes final. Include what should happen while prices load or when the system cannot get a price. A **non-goal** might be changing how the fee is calculated.

A testable **requirement** describes what must happen under a specific condition. For example, when a shopper adds a valid coupon, the review screen shows the discount and updates the total before they can confirm payment. A designer can show where that appears, an engineer can implement it, and a tester can check whether it works. “Make pricing clear” is useful as an aim but too vague to test by itself.
