Capture accessibility expectations, tracking events, and who can make decisions. Note risks and dependencies. If the price estimate comes from another system, check whether it responds fast enough on a slow connection. Write down who will investigate and what evidence would allow rollout to expand. Update the document when the team answers open questions.
Connect the roadmap to the next useful decision
A **roadmap** shows what outcomes the team plans to pursue and how it expects to sequence work. It can organize the same plan in different ways depending on what people need to decide.

value: An **outcome-based roadmap** starts with a result, such as reducing avoidable first-order cancellations.
A **theme-based roadmap** groups related ideas, such as clearer availability, honest estimates, and recovery options under “make first orders dependable.”
A **time-bounded roadmap** places work in periods, such as “test arrival ranges this quarter.” Show which items are commitments and which depend on what you learn.

blocks.value: A **backlog** contains smaller pieces of work. It can include a prototype, a tracking event to add, a reliability fix, or a delivery task. “Test whether shoppers understand arrival ranges” belongs in discovery. “Build the live stock integration” belongs in delivery when the team understands its scope, dependencies, and trade-offs.

If better estimates require live store data, make that dependency visible. Pilot the data with a few stores and decide how reliable it must be before committing to rollout. Tell stakeholders the result you want, why it matters now, and what remains open. As the evidence changes, update the sequence and explain the change.

**Practice.** Write a one-sentence outcome and one testable requirement for showing a delivery fee early. Add a non-goal and one dependency. Then describe what you would test before promising a release date.

glossary.definition: A shared document explaining the problem, intended result, and what a release needs to do.
A behavior or condition the release must meet. Clear requirements can be checked with a test.
The boundaries of the work included in the current release.
Work the team deliberately leaves out of this release.
Something your work relies on, such as a price estimate from another system.
The planned sequence of outcomes, ideas to test, and work to deliver.
The evolving list of smaller work items the team may take on.

walkthrough.title: Write a PRD and roadmap for clearer shuttle fares
walkthrough.scenario: Loop Shuttle sells shared rides for local events. Some first-time riders leave checkout after the final fare appears. Interviews suggest a late service charge surprises them, but the team needs a testable plan before it changes the fare display. The scenario and figures are fictional.

blocks.value: Give the team a measurable purpose and a scope

In a week of 300 eligible checkout starts, 75 people left after the total appeared. Several riders told support they expected a different price. That evidence points to the total display as a place to investigate. Review error logs and what alternative riders choose, because a payment failure or the actual price could also explain abandonment.

Write a product requirements document, or PRD, with the goal and who it applies to. An example outcome is to improve completed purchases among first-time riders who start checkout from 60% to 64% during a pilot. Watch refunds and fare-related support contacts. Scope covers showing the fare, service charge, discounts, and the total before payment. Changing the fare rules and adding discounts are non-goals for this release.
Turn the idea into testable requirements

value: **Valid fare.** Given a rider selects an eligible trip, show the itemized amount and the total before the Confirm purchase button. A screen reader should announce the total and any updates.
**New selection.** When the rider changes trips, mark the old price as being updated. Enable confirmation once the new total is available and the rider can review it.
**Unavailable quote.** If the pricing service cannot return a total, keep the rider's choices and offer Retry. Leave purchase unavailable until there is a valid quote.
**Record evidence.** Log a checkout start, a quote shown, a quote error, and a completed purchase. Define how to count retries so a single checkout attempt stays one attempt.
**Name the dependency and decision owner.** Engineering tests pricing response times on slow connections. Product and operations agree on which fare differences should prevent rollout.

blocks.value: Choose a roadmap view and turn it into work

An outcome-based view says “Increase successful first purchases without adding fare surprises.” A theme-based view groups quote reliability, fare explanation, and recovery under “Make pricing predictable.” A time-bounded view says “Test a prototype this month, then pilot with one event when quote reliability meets the agreed threshold.” Mark the pilot as conditional if that threshold remains open.

The backlog breaks the plan into tasks. Interview five recent abandoners, instrument the quote error event, prototype the review screen, and test the quote service under slow network conditions. A rollout task belongs after the dependency check. If the service cannot reliably return an updated price, narrow the pilot or prioritize the quote integration. Share the new sequence, the evidence behind it, and the open questions.

practice.prompt: Rewrite “Make checkout transparent” as one testable requirement, and name one event that would help evaluate whether it helps.
practice.answer: Given a rider applies a valid credit, show the credit as its own line and the updated total before purchase is available. Record that the updated quote was shown, linked to the same checkout attempt. Compare completion and support contacts for eligible attempts.

walkthrough.interview: I use a PRD to explain the problem, expected outcome, scope, and observable behavior. The roadmap sequences what we need to learn and build. The backlog contains the specific work that supports those decisions.

modules.title: Metrics, experiments, and growth
modules.summary: Read funnels and cohorts, run experiments, and choose metrics that matter.

lessons.title: Choosing metrics that reflect customer value

blocks.value: Write a metric so another person can calculate it

A **metric** is a number you use to track something. A useful definition tells two people how to get the same answer from the same data. Start by naming the result you care about. “Reliable delivery” is a goal. The share of eligible deliveries that arrive inside the window shown at checkout is one metric that can track it.

value: Set the time period and the **unit**, such as one grocery order delivered this week. Agree which orders qualify and use the original promised window the customer saw.
Count the orders that meet the condition. This is the **numerator**, the top number in the fraction. Here it is the number delivered inside that window.
Count all eligible delivered orders. This is the **denominator**, the bottom number. If 860 of 1,000 arrive inside their window, the rate is 860 ÷ 1,000 = 86%.

Agree how to handle missing delivery times and duplicate events. For example, put missing times in a separate reported group, then state whether they count as unknown or are excluded from this rate. If you exclude cancellations, report them alongside reliability so people can see when more orders fail before delivery.

blocks.value: Save the formula, data source, time period, rules, and owner in a **metric dictionary**. Walk a few orders through the calculation by hand. Include a typical order, a late one, and one with a duplicate event or missing time.
Understand what kind of number you are looking at
A grocery team improving reliability can track different parts of the work. Each kind of metric answers a different question.

value: **Input.** A resource or factor the team can influence, such as the share of stores sending usable inventory updates.
**Activity.** What someone does, such as how often stores refresh their inventory.
**Output.** What the work produces, such as the number of orders fulfilled.
**Outcome.** The result people experience, such as more orders arriving reliably or more shoppers returning.
**Guardrail.** A number that warns of an unwanted effect, such as refunds, delivery cost, or support requests.

blocks.value: Choose a North Star and look for blind spots

A **North Star metric** aims to represent value customers receive again and again. It should also have a plausible connection to the long-term health of the business. A grocery service might count weekly orders delivered in the promised window with no unresolved issue after 48 hours. Store inventory accuracy, suitable delivery slots, and completed deliveries may help drive it.

Ask how that total could rise while the service gets worse for each shopper. More new customers might produce more good orders in total, even when the percentage of orders that go well falls. Watch both the count and the percentage, along with whether people return. Set owners and limits for safety problems, support burden, refunds, and money remaining after the variable costs of an order.

For a travel app, a similar measure could count completed stays with no unresolved booking issue. Cancellations, support contacts, and money remaining per stay help show whether the growth is healthy.

**Practice.** Define a metric for “more appointments booked successfully.” Name its numerator, denominator, and time window. Add a guardrail that might worsen if you increase bookings. Check that another person could calculate it the same way.

glossary.definition: A number with a clear definition that you use to track a result or activity.
The number on top of a fraction, such as orders that arrived on time.
The number on the bottom of a fraction. It says which eligible group you are counting against.
A shared list of metrics with their formulas, rules, data sources, and owners.
A main measure of repeated customer value with a plausible link to long-term business health.
A measure that alerts you to a harmful side effect, such as a rise in refunds while order volume grows.
Money left from revenue after the variable costs you defined.

walkthrough.title: Define what a successful pickup means
walkthrough.scenario: Elm Pantry runs grocery pickup points. Managers want to track whether customers can collect a complete order at the promised time. One report counts every scanned bag as a pickup. Another counts appointments, including cancellations. The PM writes a definition that two analysts can use and compare. This exercise uses fictional data.

blocks.value: Agree on the unit, window, and counting rules

value: **Choose the unit.** Count one order, even when a clerk scans three bags for it. Use a stable order identifier to combine duplicate scan events.
**Set the window.** Count eligible completed pickups during a calendar week in the local time zone. Compare the final handoff time with the original window shown when the customer ordered.

**Define success.** A successful order is handed over within that window and has no unresolved missing-item complaint 48 hours later. Give the whole group the same 48-hour follow-up before reporting the result.

**Handle missing information.** If an order has no trustworthy handoff timestamp, count it as unknown and report that group. Decide whether the reliability denominator includes unknowns and use the same rule each week. Report cancellations separately so a rising cancellation rate remains visible.

**Save and test the definition.** Put the rules, event names, time zone, data owner, and review schedule in the metric dictionary. Reproduce a normal order, an order with a duplicate scan, and an order missing its time by hand.

blocks.value: Match each measure to a question

value.caption: Examples for Elm Pantry
rows: Share of pickup points with a working scanner
Number of checks staff make before handoff
Orders collected complete in the promised window
Cancellations and support contacts per 100 placed orders

blocks.value: A scanner upgrade can increase recorded checks while customer experience stays the same. Watch all five measures to tell whether the change reached the customer.
Use a North Star without losing sight of quality

Choose weekly complete, on-time pickups as a candidate North Star because it represents a repeated customer benefit and gives the business a result to grow. Consider two mature weeks with complete timestamps. In the first, 800 of 1,000 eligible pickups meet the definition. In the second, 900 of 1,200 do. The count rises by 100 while the rate falls from 80% to 75%. More people got a good pickup, and a smaller share of customers got one.

Review growth alongside the rate, repeat use, and cancellation and support guardrails. Assign each guardrail an owner and a threshold. Check whether failures rose at specific locations or hours before assuming demand itself is the problem.

practice.prompt: A team reports 915 successful scans out of 1,050 scans. Why is this insufficient, and what would you check before presenting a rate?
practice.answer: The unit is a pickup order, while the counts are bag scans. Deduplicate by order, check original promised and final handoff times, and wait for the 48-hour issue window. Use the agreed rules for unknowns and cancellations.

walkthrough.interview: I define the unit, numerator, denominator, time window, and edge cases before reporting a metric. I pair a customer-value count with its success rate and guardrails so growth cannot hide a worsening experience.

blocks.value: Compare two versions with A/B testing

**A/B testing** compares an existing experience with a changed version. The existing version is the **control**. The changed version is the **variant**. A random assignment decides who sees which one. This helps spread differences such as device type or shopping habits across both groups on average, so a well-run test can estimate the effect of the change.
Suppose a grocery team wants to show a clearer delivery fee breakdown. It can keep other checkout changes steady while some eligible shoppers see the old layout and others see the new one.

value: Decide who qualifies and choose a stable **assignment unit**, such as the customer account. Keep that account in the same group so repeat visits do not switch the design.

Pick a primary metric, such as the share of eligible people who start checkout and complete an order. Choose guardrails such as refunds and contribution margin. Define how much benefit would be worth the work and when to stop early for harm.

Plan the number of users and how long to run before you begin. Check that both versions record events consistently and that group sizes match the intended split closely enough. Follow the planned analysis time for a fixed-duration test.
Compare the numbers and show how uncertain the estimate is. A small effect can be measured very precisely and still be too small to justify building and maintaining the change.

blocks.value: **Worked example.** The old layout converts 60% of eligible checkout users and the new one converts 63%. The difference is 3 percentage points. Relative lift is (63 − 60) ÷ 60 = 5%.

Check what might have affected the comparison. Members of the same household could see both versions and influence each other. That is a form of **contamination**. A new screen may draw extra attention for a few days, then settle back. That is a **novelty effect**. Looking through lots of metrics or segments after the test also raises the chance of finding an apparent improvement by chance.
Diagnose a change in a metric

When a number moves unexpectedly, start by checking how you measure it. Check the event tracking, how much data you capture, who counts in the denominator, and whether the time window changed. Look at the trend before and after the shift.

Break down the result by factors that might matter, such as app version, payment method, device, geography, how users arrived, or whether they were new. A holiday, promotion, or change in the customer mix can move the total even if the experience did not change. Use only groups with enough data to interpret.

Suppose checkout completion drops from 75% to 69%. That is a fall of 6 percentage points, or 8% relative to the original rate. If the drop is concentrated in one app version and one payment method after an update, inspect its error logs and compare with versions that did not change. Report what you saw, the evidence for your explanation, what remains uncertain, and the next check or decision.

**Practice.** Checkout completion rises in your test while refunds rise too. Write how you would decide whether to expand the change. Include the result you wanted, a guardrail limit, and a check that would help explain the refunds.

glossary.definition: The group seeing the existing version of the product in a test.
The group seeing the changed version, or the changed version itself.
Using chance to decide which version each eligible participant sees.
What gets placed in a test group, such as an account, household, or store.
The difference between two percentage values. A rise from 60% to 63% is 3 percentage points.
The difference compared with the starting value. A gain of 3 points from 60% is a 5% relative lift.
An influence that crosses test groups, such as the same household using both designs.
A short-lived change in behavior caused by something feeling new.
A result that looks like a real effect even though it can be explained by chance.

walkthrough.title: Test clearer delivery fees and diagnose an unexpected drop
walkthrough.scenario: Fern Market wants to show an itemized delivery fee earlier. The team runs a controlled test, then notices a separate checkout drop after a mobile update. The same customer outcome can require different evidence in an experiment and in an investigation. All counts here are fictional.

blocks.value: Write the experiment plan before anyone sees the change

value: **Choose the population and assignment.** Include first-time customers who start an eligible checkout. Randomly assign their accounts to the existing screen or the fee breakdown. Keep each account in one group across visits.

**Define measures and timing.** Measure the share of assigned eligible accounts that complete an order within one hour of starting checkout. Guardrails include refunds and net contribution. Plan how many accounts and weeks are needed to detect a change worth the investment.

**Check the test setup.** Verify the intended group split and matching event rules. Shared accounts or people seeing both versions can contaminate the comparison. A design may also attract extra attention early, so follow the planned end date and review whether the result holds over time.

**Make a decision rule.** For illustration, require a useful improvement and uncertainty small enough to support rollout. Pause early for a clear breach of the refund guardrail. Keep planned comparisons separate from patterns noticed after searching many segments.

blocks.value: Calculate the observed lift and interpret it

Suppose 1,200 of 2,000 control accounts complete an order and 1,260 of 2,000 variant accounts complete one. The rates are 60% and 63%. Subtract to get a rise of 3 percentage points. Divide 3 by 60 for a 5% relative lift.
Absolute lift = 63% − 60% = 3 percentage points. Relative lift = 3 ÷ 60 = 5%.

Those calculations describe what happened in the sample. Check the estimated uncertainty, whether the effect reaches the agreed bar, and whether refunds or contribution worsened. If refunds increased past the guardrail, hold the release and examine which kinds of orders were affected.
Investigate a movement outside the test

A week later, a production dashboard shows checkout completion falling from 75% to 69%. Verify the event, denominator, eligibility rule, time window, and whether tracking went missing. Check the traffic mix and recent releases before assuming the fee test caused it.

Suppose 450 of 600 accounts on other versions still complete checkout, a 75% rate. Only 240 of 400 accounts on the new mobile version complete it, a 60% rate. Together they produce 690 of 1,000 completions, or 69%. This points to the new version as a place to investigate. Break it down by payment method, inspect release timing and error logs, and compare unchanged versions. Describe the cause as a hypothesis until the evidence supports it.

practice.prompt: The variant gains 3 percentage points in completion, but the refund rate rises from 2% to 4%. The team agreed refunds could rise by at most one percentage point. What is your recommendation?
practice.answer: Hold expansion. Refunds increased by two percentage points, beyond the limit. Check whether the fee breakdown changed the mix of orders or set an incorrect expectation, and investigate refund reasons before proposing another test.

walkthrough.interview: I plan an experiment around a clear outcome, fair assignment, and guardrails. When a dashboard moves outside that plan, I check measurement and isolate the affected group before attributing the change.

blocks.value: Compare groups that started at different times

A **cohort** is a group with a shared starting event or period. In a grocery app, you could group customers by the month of their first completed order. You can then compare how likely they are to place another order after the same number of days.

value: Assign each customer to the month of their first completed order.
Start their clock on that first order. Check whether they placed a second order by days 7, 30, and 60. “By day 30” includes earlier orders. “On day 30” only counts orders on that day.
Compare only groups that have had enough time to reach the day you are measuring. A group that started 10 days ago is still **immature** for a 30-day measure.

Divide the number who ordered again by the full eligible group. For a cohort of 500 customers with at least 30 days of follow-up, 150 second orders from 150 distinct customers gives a 30-day second-order rate of 150 ÷ 500 = 30%.

blocks.value: A cohort chart helps tell steady repeat use from a jump in new sign-ups. Suppose people who first ordered in September came back more often than people who first ordered in August. Check differences in promotions, areas served, customer types, and the season. A campaign might bring people who were already more likely to reorder. A controlled test or other evidence can help show whether a product change caused the difference.
Find where people stop with a funnel

A **funnel** shows how many people progress through a sequence of steps. A travel booking funnel might start with search, then track property view, room choice, guest details, payment, and confirmed booking. A big drop at payment gives you a place to look. To learn why, compare real sessions, error records, and interviews. Customers might see an unexpected price, hit a payment error, or be unsure whether to trust the site.

Before counting, define the unit, such as one customer or one checkout attempt. Use a time window and require steps in the right order. Decide what happens when a person retries or can skip a step. If your unit is one attempt, two payment clicks in the same attempt should still count as one attempt reaching payment.
**Grocery checkout example.** 1,000 view a cart → 600 begin checkout → 480 submit payment → 420 place an order.

From payment submission to order, the step conversion is 420 ÷ 480 = 87.5%. From cart view to order, end-to-end conversion is 420 ÷ 1,000 = 42%. The first question looks at people who reached payment. The second looks at the full starting group.

Look at lost users as well as the percentages. The cart-to-checkout step loses 400 people. Some may just be checking prices, so the count shows where to investigate. Compare desktop with mobile or first-time customers with returning customers. Then look for evidence about the step and group that stand out.

**Practice.** A group of 400 first-time buyers has had a full 30 days to return and 100 order again. Calculate the repeat rate, then explain what to do with a group that started five days ago. Next, name one step you would add to a checkout funnel to investigate failed payments.

glossary.definition: A group of people who share a starting event or period, such as making a first purchase in August.
A group that has not had enough time to reach the point you are measuring.
A share measured up to a point in time, such as the percentage who reordered on or before day 30.
Continued use or repeat behavior over time, measured using a definition that suits the product.
An ordered set of steps used to see how many eligible people progress or stop.
The share of eligible people who complete a target action or move to a later step.
People who reach one step but do not reach the next step within the rules you set.
The thing counted once in your calculation, such as one account or one checkout attempt.

walkthrough.title: Separate repeat bookings from checkout friction
walkthrough.scenario: TrailNest lets people book weekend cabins. The PM wants to know whether first-time customers return and where people stop during booking. Both analyses count people or attempts, but they start at different events and answer different questions. The numbers are fictional.

blocks.value: Compare cohorts with the same follow-up time

value: **Set the starting event.** Assign each customer to the month of their first confirmed cabin booking. Start their repeat clock at that booking.

**Define the return event.** Count a customer once if they make another confirmed booking by day 30. A confirmed booking on day 10 qualifies. Use confirmed bookings for the return event. Canceled bookings follow the same exclusion rule in each month.
**Wait for comparable follow-up.** Use only customers with a full 30 days. A newer group can have an early indicator, but it needs time to mature before comparing 30-day return.
**Divide by the eligible starting group.** Use the number of distinct returning customers as the numerator and all eligible first-time customers in that cohort as the denominator.

value.caption: Fictional first-booking cohorts
headers: Customers with a second booking by day 30

blocks.value: April's observed rate is six percentage points higher. Check whether the audience, prices, regions, or promotions changed. The cohort comparison can tell you when to investigate further. A controlled test can help answer whether a product change caused the difference.
Define the ordered path for a funnel

For a one-week funnel, use one booking attempt per unit. Require the steps in order within 24 hours. Combine repeated payment clicks within an attempt. Decide in advance how to handle returning to the search or going directly to a saved property, then use those rules in all segments.

value.caption: Fictional booking attempts in order

blocks.value: End-to-end conversion = 300 ÷ 800 = 37.5%. Payment-to-confirmation conversion = 300 ÷ 350 ≈ 86%.
Decide where to investigate and what evidence you need

The biggest visible loss is 280 attempts between search and cabin view. Some may be browsing. Ask whether the results show unavailable properties or prices outside the budget. Compare logs and sessions by device or first-time versus returning customers. The 50 lost after payment also deserve attention because shoppers have invested time and may be worried about their money. Inspect authorization errors and match payment attempts to confirmations.
The funnel locates friction within an attempt. The cohort analysis tells you how people behave after the first booking. Keep the denominators and clocks visible when discussing them together.

practice.prompt: May already has 12 repeat customers among 120 first-time customers after 10 days. Is it fair to compare 10% with April's 30%, and what rate should you calculate for payment errors?
practice.answer: The groups have had different amounts of time to return. Wait for May's full 30 days or compare both groups at day 10. For a payment-error rate, divide distinct attempts with a payment error by attempts that submitted payment, using the same time window and retry rule.

walkthrough.interview: I use a cohort to compare what customers do after the same starting event and follow-up time. I use a funnel to find where an ordered task breaks down, then check evidence about the reason.

lessons.title: Growth, activation, and market fit by segment

blocks.value: Follow the stages of growth

Growth includes finding customers and helping them get value over time. Teams can track five stages. The same person may move between stages at different speeds, so define an action you can measure for each one.

value: **Acquisition.** People find the product and arrive, such as from a referral or search result.
**Activation.** People first get meaningful value, such as finishing a language lesson and choosing a study goal.
**Retention.** People come back and use the product again, such as taking another lesson the next week.
**Referral.** People tell others or invite them to use the product.
**Revenue.** The product earns money, such as from a subscription or a completed order.

blocks.value: In grocery delivery, you could test whether receiving the first order in its promised window within a week of sign-up marks activation. Compare later repeat ordering among similar people who did and did not reach that milestone. Then test a change that helps more people reach it. Watch later use and order quality to see whether the benefit lasts. A relationship in the first comparison is a clue you can investigate.
Make your promise clear to the right group

**Positioning** describes whom the product serves, what they need, which other choices they consider, what benefit stands out, and why they can believe it. A travel app might serve flexible travelers who want low total prices and easy changes. Showing the full price early and describing change terms in everyday language support that promise.

For grocery delivery, busy families may compare a dependable weekly slot with picking up items in person. This focus can shape delivery features, prices, and how you describe the service. Ask people to explain the promise in their own words and tell you which alternative they would choose. Their answers can reveal whether the benefit actually matters.
See whether growth can feed itself

A **growth loop** repeats when the result of one cycle helps start the next. More local orders may attract more stores. More useful store choices may attract more shoppers. Those shoppers may bring more orders, giving stores another reason to participate.

Write down the trigger, action, result, and way it returns to the start. Estimate how many people move through each step and how long it takes. A loop can get weaker if stores run out of capacity, delivery quality falls, or promotions are abused. Check that enough value carries forward for the next cycle.
Compare customer needs with the cost to serve them

In the Peppo practice case, students might want a low-price bundle, professionals may value speed, and families may want a predictable group order. Compare how strongly each group needs the service, how much it costs to reach them, how often they order, whether they return, and how much it costs to serve them. A big audience can be hard to sustain if it is expensive to reach and rarely comes back.

Build a testable **thesis** for one group. For families, you might believe a scheduled group-order bundle will raise 30-day repeat ordering. Name the evidence behind that belief and how you will reach the group. Decide what would weaken the idea, such as repeat ordering staying flat or delivery and support costing more than the bundle earns.

**Practice.** Pick one Peppo group. Write the promise for that group and one action that shows it received value. Name one way to measure the cost to serve it and one test result that would change your plan.

glossary.definition: How people discover a product and first arrive.
The first action or result that suggests someone got meaningful value.
People continuing to use a product or returning within the period you measure.
A clear explanation of who the product is for, which alternative it competes with, and why someone would choose it.
A repeating process where one cycle produces something that helps start the next.
The cost of supporting a customer or order, such as delivery and support.
A belief about what will work and why, stated clearly enough that evidence can change it.

walkthrough.title: Choose a segment and test a repeatable growth loop
walkthrough.scenario: Peppo is a fictional meal-ordering product. The team wants to reach families who plan dinner and professionals who order after work. It can run one small pilot. The PM compares where customers get lasting value and whether the service can support the growth.

blocks.value: Give every growth stage an observable action

value: **Acquisition.** Track a new account that arrives from a campaign or a referral. Record the channel so you can compare the cost of bringing each group in.
**Activation.** Count a first meal delivered in the promised window within seven days of signup. That is an early example of the value Peppo wants to deliver.
**Retention.** Compare how many first-time customers place another order by day 30. Give each group the full window.
**Referral.** Count a successful invitation when a new customer signs up through it. Track invitations sent separately so the team can see where the process slows.
**Revenue.** Record earnings from completed orders and review contribution after variable costs, including delivery and order support.

blocks.value: If 120 of 400 new accounts activate, the activation rate is 30%. If 54 of those 120 order again within 30 days, 45% of activated customers repeat. Compare similar customers who did not activate before deciding whether a better first delivery would cause higher retention.
Position the product for a group with a clear need

A family might compare Peppo with cooking or collecting takeout. A useful promise is “Reserve dinner for the whole family and know when it will arrive.” A visible arrival window and reliable group-order fulfillment give people a reason to believe it. Ask parents to explain the promise in their own words and describe when they would still choose takeout.

Professionals might value a fast meal for one. Their alternative could be collecting food near work. A family bundle could work well for one group and make the app feel less useful for the other. Learn which need is urgent and whether the team can deliver the promise at a sustainable cost.
Draw the loop and compare economics

Suppose 25% of 120 activated customers send two invitations each, 20% of recipients sign up, and 40% of those activate. That is 30 senders, 60 invitations, 12 signups, and about five newly activated customers. Those five can start another cycle. Track how long it takes and whether delivery problems weaken referrals. In this example the loop adds customers but still needs other acquisition channels.

For an illustrative first-month comparison, family customers cost $12 each to acquire and average three orders at $5 contribution per order. That leaves $3 per acquired customer after acquisition. Professionals cost $9 and average two orders at $3 contribution, leaving a $3 shortfall. Treat the order counts as averages across each acquired group. Check sample size, later retention, and capacity before committing.

practice.prompt: Write a pilot thesis for family customers and one result that would cause you to revise it.
practice.answer: “Offering a dependable scheduled family bundle will raise 30-day repeat ordering because parents can plan dinner around a known arrival window.” Compare eligible customers with a credible baseline, and reconsider if repeat stays flat or contribution drops because deliveries need extra staff.

walkthrough.interview: I choose a segment with a clear need, define when customers first get value, and check whether they return. I compare acquisition and service costs, then test whether the proposed growth loop creates enough value to keep working.

modules.title: Case studies, portfolio, and feedback
modules.summary: Apply product thinking to realistic cases and communicate your decisions.

lessons.title: Applying the method to product cases

blocks.value: Swiggy case and finding the real problem

Imagine you are asked why so many dinner orders are canceled. First decide what you mean by “so many.” Compare the share of placed orders that are canceled in the same city and dinner hours across comparable weeks. An increase in the number of cancellations might simply mean that more people are ordering. Write down the cities, hours, dates, and customers included so everyone uses the same scope.

value: Draw what happens to one order. A customer browses, places the order, waits for restaurant acceptance, then waits for food preparation and pickup. Mark when each cancellation happened and whether the customer, restaurant, or platform canceled it.

Split the orders into useful groups, or segments. Compare first-time with repeat customers and busy with quieter hours. Ask customers and restaurants what happened at the busiest step. A chart can show where something went wrong, while an interview can help explain why.

Compare solutions for the best-supported cause. If frequent late changes to arrival estimates upset customers, test an honest delivery range. If restaurants cannot accept orders, clearer availability or a way to choose another restaurant may help more. Compare expected benefit and feasibility before choosing.

Track canceled orders divided by placed orders. Also watch conversion, delivery within the original promise, and refunds. Those guardrails help you notice whether a lower cancellation rate came at an unacceptable cost.

blocks.value: Illustrative numbers. Suppose 50 of 1,000 orders are canceled on one evening. The rate is 5%. On the next evening 60 of 1,500 orders are canceled, or 4%. The count rose but the rate fell. You would still check whether the evenings were comparable before claiming an improvement. Treat these numbers and proposed causes as exercise assumptions.
Wanderlust Travel case and discovery metrics

Start with the traveler’s journey. They get an idea, compare options, book, prepare, take the trip, and seek help if something goes wrong. Total price can matter most during comparison. Supplier reliability and schedule changes might matter after payment. A successful booking only covers one part of this journey.

If bookings fall, map the funnel from eligible searchers to selected trips to confirmed bookings. Compare people leaving soon with people planning far ahead, and compare trip types. Ask a few people who stopped what they expected to happen. If surprise fees are a common reason, test an earlier total-price estimate. If people hesitate because their plans are uncertain, test clearer or more flexible terms.

Count confirmed bookings divided by eligible searchers as a possible main measure. Check cancellations, support contacts, money left after costs, and successfully completed trips. A change that moves more people through checkout can still leave them worse off later.
GameOn case and meaningful engagement

To improve new-player return, watch a few beginners and experienced players in their first session. A beginner might spend 20 minutes on a tutorial because the goal is unclear. An experienced player might leave because the tutorial prevents them from reaching regular play. Long play time alone cannot tell these stories apart.

Test a first quest with a clear goal, such as completing a first match and knowing what to do next. Count the share of new players who return on the seventh day and check whether players completed the first match. Also look for crashes, accessibility barriers, frustration, unfair rewards, and unwanted spending. Consider whether rewards or notifications support a good first experience and whether purchases distract from it.

Try it. Choose one case and write the user group, one possible cause, the evidence you need, and one measure with a denominator. Hint. Write “out of whom?” after every count. For Wanderlust, 75 bookings out of 500 eligible searchers is 15%. That tells you the booking rate, while interviews can help you understand why others stopped.

glossary.definition: The part of the problem you are looking at, such as dinner orders in one city during a specific month.
A smaller group that shares something important to the question. New customers and repeat customers may run into different problems.
A series of steps people go through. Count how many reach each step to see where people stop.
The slowest or most limiting step in a process. If orders pile up waiting for a restaurant to accept them, acceptance may be the bottleneck.
The share of people in a group who finish a named step. Booking conversion might mean confirmed bookings divided by eligible searchers.
A measure you watch to catch a harmful side effect. If more people book but refunds rise sharply, the refund guardrail alerts you.
The share of a group that returns within a period you define. Day-7 retention here means returning on the seventh day after starting.
How practical an idea is to test or build with the time, people, tools, and information available.

walkthrough.title: Make a product decision from three different signals
walkthrough.scenario: Imagine you are reviewing three fictional product briefs with a teammate. DinnerDrop sees canceled deliveries, Trailbook sees fewer travel bookings, and Pocket League sees new players leave. Each team has room for one small test. All numbers in this walkthrough are illustrative.

blocks.value: 1. DinnerDrop. Find the cancellation you can influence

Start by naming the denominator. On Tuesday, 72 of 1,200 placed dinner orders were canceled, or 6%. On a comparable Tuesday, 96 of 1,600 were canceled, also 6%. The extra cancellations came with more placed orders. To find where to act, break the second Tuesday's 96 cancellations down by the step where they occurred.

value: Trace one order from placement to restaurant acceptance, preparation, pickup, and delivery. Of the 96 canceled orders, 60 ended before the restaurant accepted. That is 60 ÷ 96 = 62.5% of cancellations, or 60 ÷ 1,600 = 3.75% of placed orders. The first number locates the largest group. The second measures how common that issue is for shoppers.

Check who canceled and why. Compare orders by restaurant and dinner hour, and look at acceptance timestamps. A few busy restaurants may account for most early cancellations. Ask those restaurants whether they had closed ordering, missed the alert, or could no longer prepare the food.

Choose a small test that fits the evidence. If unavailable restaurants accepted orders too slowly, try pausing their listing when they mark themselves full. Check early cancellations per placed order, completed orders per visitor, and whether shoppers can find alternatives.

blocks.value: 2. Trailbook. Measure a booking from search through travel

Suppose 800 travelers run an eligible search, 200 select an itinerary, and 80 receive a confirmed booking. Search-to-booking conversion is 80 ÷ 800 = 10%. Selection-to-booking conversion is 80 ÷ 200 = 40%. The second rate helps locate a hurdle after selecting a trip. Ask people who left that step what surprised them before deciding the cause.

If interviewees repeatedly discover an added fee at payment, test an earlier total with the same suppliers. Separately track confirmed bookings per eligible searcher, cancellations per confirmed booking, support contacts, and completed trips. A fee change can move more people into checkout while the quality of the booked experience changes elsewhere.
3. Pocket League. Define engagement as something useful

Suppose 200 new players start the first session, 120 finish a match, and 36 return on day seven. First-match completion is 60%. Day-seven return is 18% of the original 200 players. Look at beginner and experienced groups with the same seven-day observation window. A long session might include confusion or a crash recovery.

**Worked decision.** Test a clearer first-match goal if observation shows beginners getting lost. Track first-match completion and day-seven return alongside crashes, accessibility issues, and unwanted spending. This connects the change to the player's first experience and keeps the team alert to side effects.

practice.prompt: Trailbook adds a price estimate. Of 800 eligible searchers, 96 receive confirmations, and the canceled share among confirmed bookings rises. What would you tell the team?
practice.answer: Confirmed bookings rose from 10% to 96 ÷ 800 = 12%, a gain of 2 percentage points. Compare with a suitable control and check how many trips actually finish. Review cancellation reasons and money left after costs before expanding.

walkthrough.interview: I would start with a rate and a clear population, then follow the user journey to find where the problem concentrates. I would interview users around that step, test a change that matches the evidence, and track both the main outcome and its side effects.

lessons.title: Building a portfolio and using feedback

blocks.value: Building a product portfolio

A portfolio is a set of examples that lets someone see how you work. Start with one case you know well. Write what people were trying to do, what got in their way, and why it mattered. Say which parts you did, which decisions the team made together, and how you knew your idea deserved a test.

value: Give the reader a starting point. For a grocery checkout case, say that first-time shoppers had trouble judging the total before payment. Describe the people you were considering and the evidence you actually had.

Show the decision. Add an artifact such as a sketch of the checkout steps or a funnel that counts how many people reached each step. Explain what alternatives you considered, such as showing a price estimate earlier or changing fee wording, and why you chose one.

Show how you would check the change. Use a KPI tree to connect the goal of more fulfilled first orders to checkout completion and successful delivery. Add a simple prototype, a research plan, or a proposed comparison test so the reader can see what you would do.

Tell the reader what happened and what remains open. For real work, report results you measured and explain your role. For a practice case, label made-up numbers and proposed steps clearly. End by saying what you would do differently.

blocks.value: A useful caption connects an artifact to the choice. For instance, “This is an example funnel with made-up numbers. It shows how I would check whether shoppers stop when the delivery fee first appears.” A reader can understand why the picture belongs in the case without assuming that you collected the data.
Mentor feedback and reflection

Ask a mentor to point to one part of the case and explain what a clearer version would show. If they say you jumped to the solution, ask which paragraph made that leap. Perhaps you showed where shoppers dropped out but gave no evidence that fees caused it. Add an interview plan to test that explanation and compare it with a possible payment error.

Choose one or two changes you can make before the next review. Write a before-and-after note. You might say, “I separated what I observed from what I assumed, and I added a second possible explanation.” Ask another reader to summarize your decision in their own words. Consider who gave the feedback and what they were trying to improve before applying it elsewhere.
Mid-fellowship check-in and learning plan

At a check-in, bring something you can demonstrate. A cohort calculation groups people by a shared starting event, such as the week they first ordered. A labeled user flow shows the steps a customer takes. Either is a clearer sign of practice than saying you finished some readings.

Use a short plan if you have fallen behind. In week one, write a metric definition and a simple experiment plan. In week two, apply both to one case and ask for feedback. Keep a note with your evidence, an unresolved question, and a next commitment with a date. For example, commit to showing a one-page fee transparency test plan at your next check-in.

Try it. Choose an existing case from the library and write four lines about the user, your role, the evidence, and your next decision. Check that a reader can tell whether the evidence was real or simulated and can point to one decision that came from it.

glossary.definition: A collection of examples that shows what you can do and how you made decisions.
A piece of work you can show, such as a journey map, sketch, spreadsheet, or experiment plan.
Something you treat as true while you look for stronger evidence. Label it so readers know it still needs checking.
Made-up numbers used to practice a method. They can show your reasoning but do not establish a real result.
A diagram that connects an important goal measure to the smaller measures that help explain it.
Something that is preventing you from making progress, such as missing data or a decision from another team.
A short review of what you learned, which evidence shows it, and what you will change next.

walkthrough.title: Turn a practice case into a portfolio someone can review
walkthrough.scenario: Imagine you are building a portfolio piece for Mapletown Library, a fictional reservation service. New visitors struggle to book a study room on their phones. Your project is a practice exercise, so the dashboard and interview notes below are simulated.

blocks.value: 1. Put your role and the decision on the first page

Open with a two-sentence brief. A new visitor wants to reserve a room before arriving. The practice data shows a drop after visitors choose an available slot, so you investigated the next step. Add a line about your role: you mapped the journey, calculated the funnel, and designed a test plan. Label the mockup and numbers as simulated. If another person drew a screen or supplied feedback, give them credit.

value.caption: Example mobile booking funnel
rows: Which visitors are eligible to book?
Which slots are missing or hard to find?
What happens between the slot and confirmation?

blocks.value: Out of 300 visitors who chose a slot, 150 confirmed, so that step converted at 50%. The overall rate is 150 ÷ 500 = 30%. Those rates locate a step worth watching. Observe users there and compare explanations, such as an unexpected account requirement, a confusing confirmation button, or a slot that disappears during checkout.
2. Build evidence around the recommendation

value: Attach a screen flow with captions that mark where visitors pause. Label each claim as an observation, a possible explanation, or a decision. For example, “Three participants stopped at the account screen” is an observation. “The screen feels unexpected” is a possible explanation to check.

Compare two choices. Showing the account requirement earlier is quick to test. Moving account creation to the end requires checking the reservation policy and may change the data flow. Choose an early explanation as the first small test if the research supports it.

Write the goal as confirmed reservations per eligible mobile visitor who starts searching. Keep a guardrail for duplicates and support requests. Describe a prototype check, the expected signal, and what result would change your recommendation.

blocks.value: 3. Translate feedback into a two-week plan

Suppose a mentor says, “I cannot tell how you got from a funnel drop to the account idea.” Ask them to point to the first unsupported claim. Update your caption to say which participants saw the account screen, add the disappearing-slot explanation, and show how to test both. Write a before-and-after sentence so the reviewer can tell what changed.

At the next check-in, bring the revised screen flow and a one-page test plan. In week one, define your metric and observe three practice sessions. In week two, update the prototype and ask a reader to explain the decision back to you. Finish the case with the next experiment you would run. Mark any untested outcome as a plan.

**Worked result.** The reader sees the same decision through four artifacts: a brief, a measured funnel, a revised screen flow, and an experiment plan. A before-and-after note gives them concrete evidence of how you used feedback.

practice.prompt: Rewrite a portfolio headline that reads “I increased mobile booking by 40%,” when you have only built a practice prototype.
practice.answer: Write “I designed a practice test for a drop in mobile room reservations.” Then say what you owned, label the illustrative funnel, and describe the comparison you would run. Save measured improvement claims for results collected after a test.

walkthrough.interview: I use the portfolio to show one decision I made and the evidence behind it. I name my role, mark simulated data, and explain what I changed after feedback. I finish with the next thing I would test.

modules.title: Technology for product managers
modules.summary: Understand APIs, Git, application layers, and system trade-offs.

blocks.value: Basics of technology and application layers

Imagine you tap Place order in a grocery app. The screen is only the first part of the trip. It takes your input and tells the rest of the system what you want. Product managers can follow that trip to find where a user problem starts and which team can help fix it.

value: The client is the website or app you see. It shows the cart, accepts a delivery choice, and displays what happened after you tap.
The service layer checks business rules. The checkout service asks whether the price, stock, and time slot are still valid and asks a payment provider to process the payment.
The data layer reads and stores facts. An order record may hold the order ID, chosen slot, and payment status so a shopper can check it later.
Infrastructure gives these pieces a place to run and a network to communicate. If a request is slow, there are several places to look, including the service, the network, or an outside provider.

blocks.value: Follow the same order when thinking about privacy and reliability. Ask who may see a delivery address, what data checkout needs, and what the customer sees when one component stops answering. A log can record that a service received a request. A metric can show how often it was slow. Together these signals help the team understand a failure, an ability called observability.
APIs

An application programming interface, or API, describes how one piece of software can ask another for something. The agreement can cover the allowed requests, required information, reply format, permissions, errors, and usage limits. A travel app might use one request to get flight options and another to book. If the fare changed between those requests, the reply should help the app explain the new price.

For stock, a grocery request could include a store and an item. The reply could say there are three left and when that count was last updated. Ask how old the count may be, who is allowed to ask, and what the shopper sees if the item is gone. When a payment request times out, the app has not heard back in time. Check the order status before encouraging a second payment, since the first may already have succeeded.
Programming languages and GitHub

Programming languages express what the system does. JavaScript can handle actions on a web page, Python can run service rules, and SQL can read or change records in a relational database. Teams choose tools based on the work and what they can maintain. Cursor is an AI-assisted editor. Review and test suggested changes before sharing them.

Git records file changes. GitHub hosts shared repositories, or collections of project files and history. An issue describes a task, a branch gives the work its own line of development, a commit records a set of changes, and a pull request lets the team review those changes. For a pending-payment message, link the pull request to the issue and show how the message appears while payment is still being checked.

Merging puts approved changes into a shared branch. Deploying puts the software into an environment where it can run. A release makes the change available to users, sometimes using a feature flag to turn it on for a test group. These can happen at different times.

Try it. A shopper sees a spinner after paying. Write the message the client should show, where the service should check for payment status, and the record that can settle whether the order exists. Hint. A pending message is useful until the system has a reliable result.

glossary.definition: The website or app a person uses. In checkout, it shows the cart and lets the shopper choose a time.
The software that carries out rules and coordinates requests. A checkout service checks stock, price, and delivery slots.
Where the product reads or keeps records such as orders, products, or delivery addresses.
The computing and network resources that keep the product running and connect its parts.
Being able to tell what a system is doing from the evidence it emits, such as logs and response times.
An agreed way for software to ask other software for information or an action. The agreement defines what goes in and what can come back.
A request waited longer than allowed for a reply. The action on the other side may still have happened.
A setting that controls which users see a feature. A team can test a change with a small group first.

walkthrough.title: Follow a ticket purchase from button to database
walkthrough.scenario: Imagine a fictional cinema app called SeatNest. A customer taps Pay for seat C8. The checkout spinner keeps running, and they are tempted to tap again. Your job is to help the team locate the problem and agree what the customer should see.

blocks.value: 1. Trace the request through four application layers

value.caption: Where each piece of checkout lives
rows: Shows seat C8 and sends the payment request
Can the screen show a clear pending state?
Checks the seat and coordinates payment
Which service owns the purchase status?
Stores the reservation ID and payment state
Runs the service and carries its requests
Where did the request spend time?

blocks.value: The client knows that the customer tapped Pay. The booking service knows whether the seat was held. The payment provider can confirm whether the charge went through. The order record links those facts to a reservation. A request log can help engineers trace one checkout, while a metric shows how often checkouts take longer than the team expects. Limit the details in logs and check who may view customer data.
2. Design the API conversation for waiting and retrying

An API is an agreement between systems. In this example, the purchase request carries a reservation reference and a payment-attempt reference. The reply includes a state such as pending, confirmed, or declined. The agreement also covers access, invalid requests, limits, and what the client can do while it waits.

value: Create the reservation reference before asking for payment. The order service can then link the result to seat C8 even if the app stops waiting.

If the app waits eight seconds without a response, show “We're checking your payment” and offer a status check. An unanswered request leaves the outcome unresolved. Check the existing reservation before presenting another payment option.
If the payment result later confirms success, show the booked seat and receipt. If it confirms a decline, explain the next step and let the customer retry deliberately.

blocks.value: 3. Make the change visible in the team's code and release

A browser client might use JavaScript to update the message. A service could use Python to check the booking rules, and SQL could read the stored status. Those are example choices. The product task is to agree how the pieces work together. If an editor suggests code, the team still reviews and tests the behavior.

Open an issue that includes the three messages and when each should appear. A developer makes a branch, records a commit, and opens a pull request on GitHub with screenshots of a delayed, successful, and declined purchase. After review and merge, the team deploys the code. A feature flag can release the new messages to a test group when support is ready.

**Worked result.** In a simulated delayed request, the provider confirms the original attempt at second 11. The client moves from pending to confirmed using the same reservation reference. The customer sees one booking and can verify the seat and receipt.

practice.prompt: At second eight the screen shows pending. At second eleven the payment provider reports success, but the order record still says pending. What should the client display?
practice.answer: Keep a truthful checking message until the system can verify and reconcile the purchase. Ask the service to check the existing reservation and payment attempt. Show a confirmed seat only once the booking record supports it. Give the customer a way to check again or get help if the wait continues.

walkthrough.interview: I map the screen, service, records, and infrastructure before deciding where to fix an issue. For payments I agree on how to represent pending states and how to check the existing attempt before any retry.

blocks.value: Git commands and collaboration basics

Suppose the app says “payment failed” before it knows what happened. Your team wants to change that message to “We’re checking your payment.” A safe change starts with its own branch. Check what is different, test the new message, record the intended edits, and share them for review.

value: Use **git branch** to see or manage branches and **git switch** to move to the one for this change. Use **git pull** when you need to bring in and integrate remote work according to the team’s settings.

Use **git status** to see which files changed and which ones are ready to commit. Use **git diff** to see the edits. Ask why any unrelated file changed and check that you have no secrets or customer data in the changes.
Use **git add** to stage the intended edits and **git commit** to record that staged version with a message such as “Clarify pending payment status.” Run the checks your team expects.

Use **git push** to share the commits and open a pull request. Reviewers can compare the old and new behavior. **git merge** combines lines of work. If two people change overlapping text and Git cannot combine it, the team resolves the conflict.

blocks.value: A product manager can check the promise in the request, the screens, and the evidence that pending, success, and failure messages each behave as intended. Engineers also check how the change works and how easy it will be to maintain. Agree on who reviews and who merges before sharing the branch.
Building technology systems

During a concert ticket sale, many shoppers arrive together. Write the path that matters most. A shopper enters the line, chooses a seat, pays, and learns whether the seat is theirs. Agree how long shoppers can wait, which actions may be retried, who will respond to trouble, and which records need to stay correct under pressure.

value: A **queue** gives work a place to wait. Show the shopper useful progress or a way to check status while the system handles work at a manageable pace.
A **rate limit** caps repeated requests. A **cache** can show a recent copy of the event description quickly. Still check authoritative seat inventory before committing to a purchase.

Payment **idempotency** lets the service recognize retries for the same payment attempt. If a shopper taps again after a slow reply, the system should check the first attempt instead of charging a second time.

blocks.value: System design in software development

A system design draws the pieces and shows how they work together. Mark where the order is accepted, where stock is checked, where the payment status lives, and where a task can wait. Draw an arrow for each request and identify which component owns each fact. Then add paths for delays, retries, and errors.

A small clinic can start with one application and one database, which may be easier to release and debug. If scheduling, messaging, and billing later need independent owners or capacity, the team can split a component. Each split adds calls between services and more ways for things to fail. Balance development speed, response time, data consistency, reliability, and cost. A grocery stock check may need an immediate reply, while a receipt email can wait briefly.

Try it. A customer retries after a slow checkout request and sees two charges. Trace the two requests. Identify one guardrail, the record that confirms what happened, and a change that makes the second request safe. Check that your fix covers a slow reply as well as a clear failure.

glossary.definition: A separate line of work in a Git project. It lets you edit and test a change before combining it with the shared branch.
Choosing which file changes will go into your next Git commit.
A case where Git cannot combine changes on its own. Someone reviews the overlap and decides what to keep.
A list of work waiting to be processed, like shoppers waiting for a turn to buy tickets.
A cap on how often a request can be made in a time period. It helps keep one user or service from crowding out others.
A fast copy of data kept for reuse. Decide how fresh the copy must be before relying on it.
Making repeat requests for the same action count as one action. A payment retry should not charge twice.
The time between making a request and receiving a reply. A quick stock check matters when someone is waiting to buy.
The record or system you trust to settle a disagreement. The payment record can show whether a shopper was actually charged.

walkthrough.title: Ship a safer payment retry during a ticket rush
walkthrough.scenario: Imagine SeatNest opens sales for a one-night show. Requests arrive faster than the checkout service can handle, and shoppers retry after a slow response. A fictional test finds two charges on one reservation. You and the engineers plan a small change and a controlled release.

blocks.value: 1. Read the code change before it reaches the shared branch

value: Start from the team's current branch according to its workflow. Use **git branch** to see your branches and **git switch** to move to the agreed work branch. When needed, use **git pull** according to the team's settings to bring remote changes into your current branch.

Run **git status** and **git diff**. Look for the retry handling and waiting message. Check for unrelated edits and any customer details or secrets. Use **git add** to stage the intended files and **git commit** to record the change with a clear message.

Use **git push** to share the branch and open a pull request. Attach two test cases, a slow successful payment and a confirmed decline. If changes overlap with another branch, resolve the conflict and rerun both tests before the team merges the change.

blocks.value: 2. Work out what the system should do under pressure

Suppose 150 checkout requests arrive in one minute and the service handles 100 per minute. If they are all accepted and all have similar cost, 50 requests remain after that minute. An orderly queue lets requests wait. A queue cannot create more processing capacity. Give shoppers an honest waiting state, and agree when to stop admitting extra work so the wait stays manageable.

A rate limit can reduce rapid repeat requests. A cache can serve the event description quickly, but seat ownership needs a check against the record that controls availability. A payment-attempt key lets the service recognize a repeat for the same purchase. The service should return the recorded outcome or indicate that work is in progress while applying the same protections against concurrent retries.
3. Draw where facts live and how to recover

value.caption: A small design for the purchase path
rows: Waiting time and the share that gives up
Two shoppers cannot both confirm the same seat
One charge for retries of the same attempt
An email delay leaves the booking status intact

blocks.value: Start with the fewest pieces that meet the system's needs. Separate receipt sending if it can wait and its failures should be recovered independently. Keep the seat check where the reservation is decided. Measure duplicate charges, checkout wait time, and support contacts after release. Make sure support can locate a purchase from its reservation reference without exposing another shopper's data.

**Worked result.** In the test, the first request completes while the client is waiting. The repeat uses the same payment-attempt key, so it reads the first result and displays the original booking. A separate test verifies that the customer can start a new attempt after a confirmed decline.

practice.prompt: If the service processes 100 requests per minute, 180 arrive in one minute, and another 50 arrive in the next, what happens to the queue under these assumptions?
practice.answer: After the first minute, 180 − 100 = 80 requests are waiting. The next minute brings 50 more, so 130 need service. Processing 100 leaves 30 waiting. This assumes requests cost about the same and the service keeps processing at capacity. Check both queue depth and how long shoppers wait.

walkthrough.interview: I would trace the retry to the authoritative payment attempt, write tests for waiting and failure, and review the code in a pull request. A queue can absorb a spike, while repeat-payment protection prevents the same attempt from creating a second charge.

modules.title: Machine learning and generative AI
modules.summary: Explore model evaluation, prompting, fine-tuning, and retrieval.

blocks.value: Introduction to machine learning

Imagine a grocery support team gets hundreds of messages. A person reads each one and chooses a category, such as refund, delivery, or account. A machine learning model can learn from past examples to suggest a category for a new message. People can correct suggestions and handle uncertain cases.

value: **Supervised learning** uses examples with known answers, or labels. A support team can train with reviewed messages and their categories.
**Unsupervised learning** looks for patterns without given labels. A team might group similar comments first and name the groups after reading them.
**Reinforcement learning** uses rewards to learn what actions to take over time. In a delivery simulation, a routing system could earn a reward for making deliveries on time.

blocks.value: Decide which information is available at the time the model makes its suggestion. A delivery prediction can use courier availability before dispatch. It should not use the actual arrival time, which is only known afterward. Keep a separate set of examples out of training so you can see how the model handles cases it did not learn from. Include recent examples to check whether a policy or demand change made older patterns less useful.
Common ML algorithms

Pick a method based on what answer you need. To estimate delivery minutes, **linear regression** learns how inputs relate to a number. To estimate the chance of a late delivery, **logistic regression** can predict the probability of a category. Use a **decision tree** when you want to think in splits, such as “Is the distance over five kilometers?” A **random forest** combines predictions from many trees. **Gradient boosting** builds a series of trees that improve the combined predictions.

**Clustering** groups similar records. A **recommender** ranks choices, such as items a customer may want to reorder. **Neural networks** learn through layers and can work with complex information such as text or images. Compare any method with a baseline. A complex model needs to do useful work that a simpler rule cannot do as well.

value: Suppose 5 of 100 deliveries were late. A baseline that says every order is on time is 95% accurate, yet catches none of the late orders.
Suppose your new model flags 8 orders and 4 of them are late. Recall is 4 out of 5, or 80%. Precision is 4 out of 8, or 50%.

Ask if the team can investigate eight flags quickly. Check whether staff can understand a flag, and what happens when a late order is missed. Include response time and maintenance effort in the decision.

blocks.value: Generative AI

Generative AI makes content such as text, images, audio, or code. A grocery support assistant can draft a reply using a verified order record and an approved refund policy. Set a standard for the draft. The order details and policy must match the sources, the next step must be useful, and a person should review sensitive cases. Test whether the draft accidentally exposes private data or promises a refund the policy does not allow.

Try it. A system flags 10 orders. Six flags are right, and eight orders really were late. Calculate precision and recall. Check. Precision is 6 out of 10, or 60%. Recall is 6 out of 8, or 75%. Say which number matters most if missing a late order is expensive.

glossary.definition: Using data to learn patterns that help predict, group, or rank new examples.
The known answer attached to an example, such as “refund” on a support ticket.
Training on examples that have known answers. The model learns to predict a label or number for a new example.
Looking for patterns in data without supplying correct answers, such as grouping similar customer comments.
Learning which actions to choose using rewards from earlier choices, often over several steps.
A simple method you compare with a new method, such as a rule that flags a late order if its estimate exceeds the promise.
Out of all the cases you wanted to catch, the share you did catch. If you flag four of five late orders, recall is 80%.
Out of all the cases you flagged, the share that really matched. Four late orders in eight flags gives 50% precision.
A model that creates new content such as a draft reply, an image, or code from input you give it.

walkthrough.title: Choose a model for missed delivery promises
walkthrough.scenario: Imagine FreshTrail, a fictional delivery service, wants to warn support staff before a grocery order runs late. The team also wants a draft message that support can edit. A prediction about the delivery and a written explanation are two separate jobs. The sample counts below are illustrative.

blocks.value: 1. Decide what the machine should learn

A supervised model uses examples with answers. For each old order, you can label whether it arrived after the promise. At dispatch time, useful inputs might include the delivery distance, pickup backlog, and couriers available. The actual arrival time belongs in the label because it is known later. Hold out a later group of orders for evaluation and check whether holidays or policy changes make the old examples less representative.

Unsupervised learning could group past complaints with similar patterns, and a researcher could name those groups afterward. Reinforcement learning could explore dispatch choices in a simulation, with rewards for on-time arrivals and penalties for costs. The quality of the simulation and reward matters because the system learns from the consequences it sees.
2. Match the method to the decision

value.caption: Candidate methods for different FreshTrail questions
rows: How many minutes will this delivery take?
Predict a number from inputs such as distance.
How likely is it to be late?
Estimate the probability of a late delivery.
Which conditions make this order risky?
Use readable splits such as distance and pickup backlog.
A forest combines trees. Boosting adds trees that improve the previous prediction.
Group similar records and inspect the groups.

blocks.value: Neural networks can learn from complex inputs such as text or images. Compare any model with a simple baseline, such as a flag for orders still waiting at a busy pickup location. Ask about accuracy, speed, data needs, and maintenance before choosing the more complex model.
3. Evaluate whether the result helps support

value: Count the actual late deliveries. If 10 of 200 are late, a baseline predicting all orders on time is 190 ÷ 200 = 95% accurate and flags zero late orders.
Suppose a model flags 12 orders and 8 are late. Precision is 8 ÷ 12, about 67%. Recall is 8 ÷ 10 = 80%. A support lead now knows that four flags are false alarms and two late orders were missed.
Set an action for a flag and verify staff can manage the volume. Check performance on different regions, weather, or pickup conditions before expanding.

blocks.value: A generative model could draft the notification after a flag. Give it the verified order status and approved wording, and have staff review sensitive cases. Test whether it invents an arrival time or promises compensation the rules do not support.

**Worked decision.** Pilot the alert with staff and compare the time to investigate with the current workflow. Score the prediction and the draft separately. A useful alert can come with a draft that still needs revision.

practice.prompt: A later model flags 20 orders. Nine of those flags are correct, and there were 12 late orders. Calculate precision and recall.
practice.answer: Precision is 9 ÷ 20 = 45%. Recall is 9 ÷ 12 = 75%. Eleven false alarms now require staff attention. Compare both rates and workload before choosing this model.

walkthrough.interview: I first decide whether the task needs a prediction or generated content. I compare a simple baseline and use measures that reflect the cost of errors. Then I test the human workflow that acts on the model's output.

lessons.title: Language models, prompts, and failure modes

blocks.value: Large language models (LLMs)

A large language model, or LLM, usually writes one token at a time. A token can be a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark. The model looks at the instructions, conversation, and other information it was given. It estimates what could come next. The model and its decoding settings affect which continuation is selected.

Say you ask it to summarize 500 grocery reviews. It can describe a common complaint in clear language, but it might get the number of complaints wrong. Count categories using a spreadsheet or code. Give the model those verified totals and ask it to explain them. Check that any quote matches the review and remove private details first. For current order facts, use a tool that reads the live record.
Prompt engineering

Prompt engineering means making the task clear and checking whether the instructions work. A prompt for a support classifier should say what the labels mean, what information is allowed, and what happens when a message does not provide enough evidence. Compare prompt versions on the same easy and difficult examples.

value: State the task. “Read the message and identify why the customer contacted us.” Define delivery, refund, and account with a few examples. Decide whether more than one label is allowed.
Ask for a label and the phrase that supports it. Allow “unknown” if the message is too vague. Use a JSON schema to tell the application which fields and values are allowed.

Check form and meaning separately. The schema can catch “billing-other” if that label is not allowed. A reviewer can catch a real delivery problem mislabeled as a refund even though the answer had a valid form.
