cases.title: GroveCart and the retention drop
cases.summary: Find out why 30-day repeat ordering fell from 50% to 40% while both acquisition channels improved.

blocks.value: The decision

GroveCart, a fictional grocery service, redesigned first checkout in February and expanded a partner promotion. The product lead wants to revert checkout because overall 30-day repeat ordering fell. Marketing wants to double the promotion. You have two fully matured cohorts, grouped by first completed order and acquisition channel.

First order | Channel | Customers | Reordered by day 30
January     | Organic |       200 |                 120
January     | Partner |       100 |                  30
February    | Organic |       100 |                  64
February    | Partner |       300 |                  96
Your task

value: Calculate repeat rates for each month and channel. Compare February at January’s channel weights.
Explain what the observed data can tell you about the checkout redesign and the promotion.
Recommend a decision this week, one guardrail, and which team should own the follow-up.

solution.value: Separate the total from the mix

January was 150 ÷ 300, or 50%, and February was 160 ÷ 400, or 40%. Organic rose from 60% to 64% and partner rose from 30% to 32%. Applying January’s two-thirds organic and one-third partner weights gives February about 53.3%. The larger share of partner customers, who repeat at a lower rate in both months, explains how the combined rate can fall while both channel rates rise.

-- One row per first-order customer
SELECT first_order_month, channel, COUNT(*) AS customers,
       SUM(reordered_by_day_30) AS repeats,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(reordered_by_day_30) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_pct
FROM customer_cohorts
WHERE eligible_for_day_30 = 1
GROUP BY first_order_month, channel
ORDER BY first_order_month, channel;

Keep checkout stable while you investigate unless another guardrail requires a rollback. Use a controlled test to estimate the redesign’s impact. Ask marketing and finance to compare partner and organic acquisition cost and 30-day contribution before expanding the promotion. Assign analytics to validate event coverage and operations to check whether service quality differs by channel. Review at a scheduled decision meeting when the next cohort matures.
**Watch for.** Improved repeat ordering within a channel can still reflect changes in region, customer intent, or incentives. Treat the fixed-mix result as a diagnostic.

cases.deliverable: A one-page retention memo with a grouped SQL query, the fixed-mix calculation, and a dated follow-up plan.

cases.title: RelayDesk chooses its first market
cases.summary: Use trial, activation, retention, and buying evidence to choose between a broad market and a stronger early niche.

blocks.value: The decision

RelayDesk is a fictional help-desk product. Independent teams generate most trials. Compliance-sensitive support teams start fewer trials and frequently cite audit history as the reason they switch. The next quarter has one engineering team and one customer-success lead available.

Segment                      | Trials | Activated | Active at day 60 | Paid
Independent teams            |    400 |       120 |               48 |   60
Compliance-sensitive support |    120 |        60 |               42 |   35

All trial cohorts have completed 60 days. Activation means closing three real tickets as a team in week one. Sales estimates 700 reachable compliance-sensitive accounts, a 25% pilot acceptance rate, and 55% pilot-to-paid conversion at $9,000 per annual account. Buyers often request single sign-on, audit exports, and a predictable implementation timeline.
Your task

value: Choose one segment and explain what makes the evidence persuasive or incomplete.
Estimate annual recurring revenue under the sales assumptions. Identify two assumptions to validate.
Write a pilot objective and two results that would justify the next investment.

solution.value: Choose compliance-sensitive support for a bounded pilot. Trial activation is 50% compared with 30%, day-60 active rates are 35% compared with 12%, and paid conversion is about 29% compared with 15%. This is stronger observed evidence of team-level value. Different sales involvement or recruitment could explain some of the gap. Interview lost deals and stalled trials as well as customers that adopted.

The estimate is 700 × 25% × 55% × $9,000, or about $866,250 in annual recurring revenue at expected values. Test whether the accounts are genuinely reachable and whether the buying cycle supports the pilot-to-paid assumption. Model acquisition, implementation, and support costs before treating the opportunity as viable.

value: Set the objective of making audit-ready support workflows valuable within a small group of new accounts.
For a 20-account pilot, set targets such as at least 12 accounts activating in week one and at least 8 remaining active at day 60. Use account-level rows and aggregate by segment and pilot cohort.

Have sales own recruitment, engineering own the required controls, and customer success record implementation hours and blockers. Agree on the minimum launch scope and a day-60 review before taking on more accounts.

solution.value: **Watch for.** These targets are pilot decision criteria. With 20 accounts, report counts and uncertainty alongside percentages.

cases.deliverable: A segment recommendation, a transparent revenue model, and a small pilot plan with owners and measurable results.

cases.title: CivicRoute races an appointment deadline
cases.summary: Use conversion evidence and a dependency map to scope a booking pilot that preserves access when schedules fail.

blocks.value: The decision

CivicRoute is a fictional local-service appointment site. It plans to pilot same-week slots in one district in ten working days. The current mobile booking funnel is weaker than desktop. The sponsor also asks for an interactive office map before launch.

Device  | Booking starts | Confirmed bookings
Mobile  |            200 |                112
Desktop |            160 |                120

Work item               | Days | Starts after
Calendar access         |    4 | Project start
Booking integration     |    3 | Calendar access
End-to-end regression   |    2 | Booking integration
Plain-language content  |    2 | Project start
Localization review     |    3 | Plain-language content

An optional survey after abandonment drew 52 responses. Thirty-four reported no suitable time, 11 found the location unclear, and seven gave other reasons. The call center can still book appointments if online slots are unavailable. The pilot must work with keyboard navigation and preserve a clear phone alternative.
Your task

value: Identify the likely launch constraint, total duration, and amount of schedule buffer.
Decide how to respond to the office map request. Define two acceptance criteria and a rollback trigger.
Specify a query or aggregation to measure the pilot without combining different booking paths.

solution.value: The calendar, integration, and regression chain takes nine working days, leaving one day before the planned pilot. The content and localization chain takes five days if it can run in parallel. Confirm reviewer availability and put keyboard and fallback scenarios inside the scheduled regression work.

Mobile conversion is 56%, versus 75% on desktop. The survey suggests timing is worth investigating and location is a real concern for some respondents. Start with clear office addresses and instructions, then test the larger map request separately. Its relative benefit and dependencies should be visible before it enters scope.

value: Given a valid slot, a person using only a keyboard can select it and receive a confirmation that states the office and local time.
Given a calendar timeout, show an understandable message and a working phone alternative without confirming an unreserved slot.

Pause online rollout if confirmed appointments are missing from the calendar or duplicate bookings appear. Give the launch lead authority to pause and the operations lead responsibility for the phone fallback.

Group a table with one row per online booking attempt by device and time period, and calculate confirmed attempts divided by started attempts. Report phone bookings and wait time as separate operational measures.

cases.deliverable: A pilot scope, a dependency plan, and a release checklist with accessibility, monitoring, and fallback owners.

cases.title: Workshop considers a higher subscription price
cases.summary: Calculate first-month contribution per eligible visitor and make a rollout decision with incomplete retention evidence.

blocks.value: The decision

Workshop, a fictional scheduling tool for makerspaces, tests a higher monthly price. It randomly assigns 1,000 eligible new visitors to two versions. Existing subscribers retain their price. Each new paid account costs $6 to serve in its first month. Assume no credits, refunds, or non-payer variable costs in this simplified dataset.

Version | Eligible visitors | Paid in month 1 | Monthly price | Active at day 60
A       |               500 |              90 | $20           |               50
B       |               500 |              73 | $26           |               40
Your task

value: Calculate paid conversion, contribution per eligible visitor, and day-60 activity among paid accounts.
Choose whether to keep testing, roll out, or reverse. Describe an uncertainty that affects your decision.
List the billing and support checks required before expanding the test.

solution.value: Paid conversion falls from 18.0% to 14.6%. A contributes 90 × ($20 − $6) = $1,260, or $2.52 per eligible visitor. B contributes 73 × ($26 − $6) = $1,460, or $2.92 per eligible visitor. First-month contribution improves by $0.40 per eligible visitor. Compare the effect and its uncertainty at the same decision unit that was randomized.

Day-60 activity among paid accounts is 50 of 90, or 55.6%, for A and 40 of 73, or 54.8%, for B. B also produces fewer day-60 active accounts per assigned visitor, 8% versus 10%. Paid accounts are selected after assignment and can differ between versions, so the conditional retention rates need care. With the limited evidence, keep the test bounded or run a confirmatory test with an agreed analysis plan and sufficient follow-up before expanding.

value: Join one assignment per visitor to a first-month billing summary by visitor ID. Include eligible non-payers with zero contribution and report refunds and credits explicitly.
Have billing confirm a stable assigned price through checkout, invoices, renewal, cancellation, and retries. Confirm existing subscribers stay on their agreed price.
Have support track pricing confusion and refund requests. Agree when to stop for billing errors or review the contribution and customer guardrails together.

cases.deliverable: An experiment readout showing both prices, the arithmetic, the recommended next test, and rollout prerequisites.

cases.title: Patchbay prioritizes a marketplace fix
cases.summary: Score three ideas, account for an unverified inventory dependency, and choose a plan with four person-weeks available.

blocks.value: The decision

Patchbay is a fictional musical-equipment rental marketplace. It saw 65 stock-related cancellations in 1,000 checkout attempts last month. Some suppliers update availability in batches. Support would like more self-service options, and sellers ask for easier photo uploads. The team has four person-weeks in the next cycle.

Candidate                 | Reach | Impact | Confidence | Effort (person-weeks)
Temporary inventory holds |   800 |    1.0 |        70% |                     3
Support self-service      |   800 |    0.5 |        80% |                     2
Easier seller uploads     |   150 |    1.0 |        60% |                     1

Reach is estimated monthly exposure in the affected audience. Impact uses a shared scale for the product goal of reliable completed rentals. The holds estimate assumes suppliers can expose timely availability. One supplier has yet to confirm this. Long holds could block other customers from booking.
Your task

value: Calculate the three RICE scores and identify an assumption that could change the ordering.
Recommend how to use the four weeks, including a fallback if the supplier dependency fails.
Name the events and guardrails you would need to distinguish a genuine reliability improvement from reduced availability.

solution.value: The estimates are about 187 for temporary holds, 160 for support self-service, and 90 for uploads. At 50% confidence, the holds score drops to about 133. Start with a one-week technical spike to check freshness and whether repeated requests can safely reuse an existing hold. If the spike succeeds, use the remaining three weeks for a bounded pilot. If it fails, prioritize self-service and use the remaining week to investigate which supplier workflows could provide fresher data.

Define acceptance criteria for creating, expiring, releasing, and retrying a hold. A delayed payment must either convert a valid hold to a booking or show a clear fallback. Use hold and booking IDs to join records without counting retries as separate checkout attempts. Segment stock-related cancellation rates by supplier and inventory freshness.

value: Measure stock cancellations per eligible checkout attempt and total completed rentals.
Monitor how often a shopper cannot book because another shopper is holding the item and how long stock remains reserved after abandonment.
Give operations a supplier-level switch and an owner who can stop the pilot if it leaves items locked or allows conflicting bookings.

cases.deliverable: A scoring table with a sensitivity check, a dependency decision, and pilot metrics for buyers and suppliers.

cases.title: RedBridge reviews an AI assistant before launch
cases.summary: Decide whether a better-scoring support assistant meets the quality and safety bar for customer-facing use.

blocks.value: The decision

RedBridge is a fictional electronics support team. Its AI assistant retrieves approved documents and drafts answers for staff. Two versions ran in shadow mode on the same 120 held-out tickets. A correct answer supported by the sources or an appropriate escalation counts as fully correct. An unsupported credit instruction counts as severe. No draft was sent to a customer.

Version | Evaluated | Fully correct or escalated correctly | Severe errors
A       |       120 |                                  102 |             1
B       |       120 |                                  110 |             0

The agreed launch rule is at least 95% fully correct and zero severe errors on the evaluation set. A sponsor wants to ship B because it improved. Staff still say several drafts are difficult to verify quickly when a ticket references an old return policy.
Your task

value: Make a launch decision and explain how the data supports it.
Propose an evaluation slice and two safeguards that address the known risks.
Assign owners for a follow-up test, a supervised pilot, and a pause decision.

solution.value: Keep B in shadow mode. It scored 110 ÷ 120, or 91.7%, compared with 85% for A. It would need at least 114 correct tickets to reach the 95% threshold. Zero severe failures in this sample satisfies that observed requirement. More targeted testing is needed to understand the chance of a severe failure in use.

value: Add cases with overlapping policy versions, missing order details, ambiguous eligibility, and conflicting sources. Check whether the assistant retrieves the applicable document and makes escalation easy when evidence is weak.
Keep access to sensitive account actions outside the drafting tool. Require human review for messages involving credits, refunds, or policy exceptions.

Assign analytics to aggregate results by test version and risk category, engineering to implement safeguards, and support to assess verification time and agent edits. Appoint a rollout lead who can stop a supervised pilot.

solution.value:
-- One reviewed result per ticket and version
SELECT model_version, risk_category, COUNT(*) AS reviewed,
       SUM(CASE WHEN outcome = 'fully_correct' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS correct,
       SUM(CASE WHEN severity = 'severe' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS severe
FROM evaluation_results
WHERE dataset = 'held_out'
GROUP BY model_version, risk_category;
**Watch for.** Use consistent labels when an appropriate escalation is counted as correct. Keep the held-out data separate from examples used to revise the system.

cases.deliverable: A release decision with an evaluation table, risk safeguards, and an owner for each follow-up action.

rice.title: RICE framework in product management
rice.scenario: Imagine you manage part of Swiggy’s food-ordering experience. Your team has four ideas and time to begin one. Your shared goal is to increase monthly completed orders. You want a consistent way to compare the ideas and a record of where you are making assumptions. The numbers in this guide are fictional.

blocks.value: What RICE helps you decide

RICE helps a product manager choose which feature ideas to consider first when time is limited. It looks at how many people a feature can affect, the change you expect for each person, the quality of the evidence, and the work the team would need to do. Start by agreeing on the customer problem and the result you want. Then compare the ideas that address it.
RICE score = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort

Use a common time period, impact scale, and effort unit across the list. In this guide, reach is the number of users affected in a month. The impact scale refers to completed orders. Effort is the combined work in person-months.
R means reach

Reach asks how many users would encounter or be affected by the change in your chosen period. Suppose 100,000 people visit the menu discovery screen each month, and you expect half of them to see the new recommendations. That makes reach 100,000 × 0.5 = 50,000 users per month. Count distinct users if that is the unit you chose. Ten visits from the same person still represent one user.
I means impact

Impact asks how much the change could help one person who encounters it. Use the same outcome for every feature so the scores mean the same thing. For recommendations, the team expects people to find a meal faster and complete more orders, so it assigns a High impact of 2. An impact of 2 is a rating on a shared scale. A pilot can measure the actual change in orders later.

value.caption: Common RICE impact ratings

blocks.value: C means confidence

Confidence asks how much evidence supports the reach, impact, and effort estimates. Menu usage data helps estimate reach, and early research suggests people struggle to choose a meal. The team still needs to test whether recommendations increase orders. It gives this idea Medium confidence of 80%. In the calculation, use 0.8 for 80%.

value.caption: Common RICE confidence ratings
rows: Strong usage data, customer evidence, and a team estimate
Some evidence, with a major assumption still to test
Early signals and several uncertain estimates

blocks.value: E means effort

Effort asks how much team time the change will take. Add the work across product, design, engineering, analytics, and testing where they contribute. One person working for one month is one person-month. Two people working for two months add up to four person-months, even though only two calendar months pass. Suppose the team estimates four person-months for recommendations.
Calculate the RICE score for recommendations

value: Multiply reach by impact. 50,000 × 2 = 100,000.
Apply confidence. 100,000 × 0.8 = 80,000.
Divide by effort. 80,000 ÷ 4 = 20,000.

blocks.value: AI recommendations = 50,000 × 2 × 0.8 ÷ 4 = 20,000

decision: Start by considering faster checkout. It scores 40,000 because the team expects a strong effect on completed orders and can build it in three person-months. Dark mode reaches more people, but the team expects a smaller effect on this particular goal. A different goal could change the impact ratings.

Use the ranking to start the decision. Check for work that must happen first. For example, checkout might depend on a required payment security fix. Record that dependency, the reason it changes the order, and the date when the team will reconsider. For each scored feature, record which assumption you would test before spending the full effort.

practice.prompt: Suppose design research lowers confidence in AI recommendations from 80% to 50%, and the revised plan needs five person-months. Calculate the new score and compare it with dark mode.
practice.answer: Multiply 50,000 × 2 × 0.5 to get 50,000. Divide by five person-months to get a RICE score of 10,000. Under these assumptions, dark mode’s 12,000 score moves ahead. The ranking changed because the recommendation idea now has weaker evidence and needs more effort.

rice.interview: I use RICE to compare candidate solutions after we agree on the customer problem. I estimate how many users each change will reach in the same period, score the impact on a shared goal, adjust for confidence in the evidence, and divide by total team effort. I review the ranking with the team and account for dependencies, strategy, and required work before choosing what to start.

glossary.definition: The number of people or events a change affects during a defined period, such as 50,000 users in one month.
The expected effect on the chosen result for each person who encounters the change.
How much evidence supports your estimates. Use 80% as 0.8 in the formula.
The total work across the people needed to deliver the change.
One person’s work for a month. Two people working full-time for two months contribute four person-months.
Work that must happen first so another task can start or finish.
